text: Which of the following would be wrong for a Product Owner to do? Select the best answer.
options: Determine the timing for releasing the product Increment.
Approve the work completed during the Sprint.
Set the Sprint Goal without consulting the team.
Set a Product Goal.
trap: Do not confuse the Product Owner's accountability for maximizing value with an authoritarian role during team events.
explanation: Correct: 'Set the Sprint Goal without consulting the team.' The Sprint Goal is collaboratively defined by the entire Scrum Team (Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers) during Sprint Planning. It cannot be set unilaterally by the Product Owner.

text: As a Product Owner in scaled Scrum with multiple Scrum teams, what approach would be most beneficial when you are unable to dedicate enough time to each team? (choose the best option)
options: Assemble a group of Proxy Product Owners from the current Scrum Team members.
Ensure all Scrum Teams have a thorough grasp of the Product Vision, so they can be guided by it if you delegate certain tasks to the Developers.
All the above options are valid; the decision depends on the specific situation.
Hire additional Product Owners for every product component.
Collaborate with the Program Management Office to receive the necessary support.
trap: Proxy Product Owners and multiple component POs are anti-patterns in Scrum. There is only ever one Product Owner per product.
explanation: Correct: 'Ensure all Scrum Teams have a thorough grasp of the Product Vision...' According to Scrum, a product has only one Product Owner. If the PO is overloaded, they can delegate certain tasks to the Developers, but they remain accountable. A clear and strong Product Vision enables the teams to self-manage effectively.

text: As the Product Owner you realise the last increment did not meet the full Definition of Done and you are concerned about its quality. What is the likely result? (choose all that apply)
options: The next Sprints velocity may be interrupted when quality issues are encountered.
The indication of progress on the Product Backlog is not transparent.
The project manager cannot effectively update the plan.
The incomplete Sprint Backlog items should be returned to the Product Backlog.
The Increment should not be released.
trap: Scrum does not recognize the role of a traditional Project Manager, so options referring to a project manager's plan are incorrect.
explanation: Correct: If an increment does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released, and it cannot be presented at the Sprint Review. The incomplete items are returned to the Product Backlog. Progress metrics become non-transparent, and future velocity will be hit by tech debt and quality issues.

text: The Developers in the company you work at complain that they feel frustrated by constant interruptions and useless meetings, and much of their past work has resulted in being unneeded. You notice that some of your best Developers are leaving. What measurements should you consider for informing you on how to improve employee retention rates? (choose the best answer)
options: The Innovation Rate, which is the ratio of new work to total work.
All of the above.
The On-Product Index, which measures the proportion of work related to the product to total work.
Employee Net Promoter Scores, which measures the overall job satisfaction and company satisfaction of the developers.
trap: Do not look for a single isolated metric. Employee retention and satisfaction are multi-faceted.
explanation: Correct: 'All of the above.' Innovation Rate, On-Product Index, and Employee Net Promoter Scores are all official metrics within the Evidence-Based Management (EBM) framework that help evaluate employee satisfaction, waste, and organizational health.

text: Which of the following are true about Scrum? (Select all that apply).
options: Each element of Scrum serves a distinct purpose and is crucial for the successful application of Scrum in building complex products.
Scrum is similar to traditional processes, with the key difference being self-management replacing Project Managers.
Scrum is a methodology that allows you to selectively implement components based on your organization's specific needs.
Scrum is founded on the principles of empiricism.
Scrum is a framework designed to deliver value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.
trap: Scrum is explicitly defined as a lightweight framework, not a 'methodology', and is not a buffet where you can selectively pick components.
explanation: Correct: Scrum is an empirical framework designed for adaptive solutions. While selective implementation of parts of Scrum is possible, the resulting system is not Scrum. Each defined element is essential.

text: Who has accountability for clearly expressing the Product Backlog Items? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Master, with the option to enlist the Product Owner's assistance.
The Scrum Master, with the option to enlist the Developers' assistance.
The Product Owner, who can designate a team member within the Scrum Team to handle the task.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
trap: Accountability can never be transferred, even if the execution of the task is delegated.
explanation: Correct: The Product Owner is solely accountable for Product Backlog management, which includes clearly expressing items, although they may delegate the execution of these tasks to others.

text: Scrum is about getting started, the right product will emerge eventually. True or False?
options: False
True
trap: Do not overthink. Scrum values action and iterative learning over extensive upfront analysis.
explanation: Correct: True. Scrum is built on empiricism. You cannot know everything upfront; you begin with a basic understanding and the right product features emerge as you release increments and gather feedback.

text: In Scrum every .... needs a Product Owner. Choose from the below to fill in the blank.
options: Program
Product
Portfolio
Project
trap: Do not confuse project-based management with product-centric Scrum frameworks.
explanation: Correct: Product. In Scrum, every Product must have exactly one Product Owner and one Product Backlog, regardless of how many Scrum Teams work on it.

text: Who tells the Developers how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value?
options: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master
None of the above
The Lead Developer
trap: No hierarchical authority tells the Developers how to perform their technical tasks in Scrum.
explanation: Correct: 'None of the above'. Developers are completely self-managing. They alone decide how to turn Product Backlog items into functional, valuable Increments.

text: If Sprint Backlog items are not clear what might be the concerns? (choose the best 4 answers)
options: Development time might be wasted.
The Scrum Master has failed, the Scrum Master is changed and the Sprint is re-started.
There is no concern, the Developers do not need the items to be clear.
The team might have different understandings and different basis for adaptation.
Decisions made on those items may be bad decisions.
The Developers will have difficulty creating a forecast of work for the Sprint without more clarity.
trap: Scrum does not punish Scrum Masters by instantly changing them, nor does it dismiss the need for clarity.
explanation: Correct: Lack of clarity causes waste of development effort, differing assumptions about adaptation, poor decision-making during implementation, and major challenges for forecasting during Sprint Planning.

text: Which is the best description of the Sprint Backlog as a result of Sprint Planning? (choose the best answer)
options: It is a decomposition of Product Backlog items such that enough work is decomposed for at least the first days of the Sprint.
It is an exhaustive list of all tasks for the Sprint.
It is a list of the User Stories estimated in story points, and a list of corresponding tasks that are estimated in hours.
It is a task list where every Developer has signed up for all the tasks that they intend to do in the Sprint.
It must be ordered by the Product Owner.
trap: The Sprint Backlog is not a static, exhaustive task list. It emerges continuously throughout the Sprint.
explanation: Correct: The Sprint Backlog must have enough detail so the Developers can forecast and start working on the first few days of the Sprint. The rest of the work is decomposed as the Sprint progresses.

text: Upon discovering that several features considered important have low usage, what actions should a Product Owner take to investigate this issue? (choose all that apply)
options: Examine whether underutilized features effectively address the intended problem.
Carry out experiments to gain a better understanding of what customers value.
Spend more time communicating with users to sell the benefits of the features.
Disable seldom-used features and collect feedback.
trap: Trying to advertise or 'sell' a feature that customers do not want is a push-strategy that contradicts empirical, value-driven management.
explanation: Correct: Examining whether features actually solve the problem, running experiments to learn what customers value, and safely disabling underused features to gauge reactions are all strong empirical approaches.

text: A new social media app has entered the market and is starting to steal customers away from your company's primary social media product. Your competition releases new and useful features quicker than you can and their customers are more satisfied. You realise you need to improve your T2M. How can you do this? (choose all that apply)
options: Taking control of and improve the delivery pipeline.
Reducing the number of features in each product release.
Use automation to improve speed.
Removing internal communication bottlenecks.
Removing activities that do not add value to the development and delivery process.
trap: All of these options are valid methods to optimize Time-to-Market (T2M) by reducing cycle times and eliminating waste.
explanation: Correct: All options are correct. Optimizing T2M requires improving pipelines, automating manual processes, working in smaller batches (less features per release), and removing non-value-adding communication and process bottlenecks.

text: The Scrum Master is inexperienced and suggests that Developers with rare skills should be involved with multiple Scrum teams. Which are likely outcomes from such a decision? (choose all that apply)
options: Teams may become 'bottlenecked' waiting for key Developers.
Employee costs are lower since expensive skilled employees are shared.
Teams will not be cross-functional.
Dependencies are created.
More work gets done since people with specialisms are better utilized.
trap: Sharing specialists might seem cost-efficient on paper, but it introduces huge friction, delays, and context-switching costs.
explanation: Correct: Sharing specialists across teams creates severe scheduling dependencies, leads to resource bottlenecks, and compromises the cross-functional, self-contained nature of individual Scrum Teams.

text: A 'cone of uncertainty' can be used for? (choose the best answer)
options: Determining whether to cut quality, similar to the 'Iron Triangle' of project management.
Rapidly identifying and prioritizing all uncertainties.
Visualizing the uncertainty of the potential value that a Scrum Team delivers over time.
Representing the relative level of difficulty for predicting the velocity of individual team members.
trap: Do not use the Cone of Uncertainty to justify cutting quality. Quality standards (Definition of Done) must remain high.
explanation: Correct: The 'cone of uncertainty' shows how uncertainty about scope, schedule, and potential delivered value decreases over time as more data and empirical evidence are gathered.

text: Managing the Product Backlog involves which of the following? (choose all that apply)
options: Ordering the items by priority.
Reviewing the Product Backlog items with stakeholders.
Breaking large Product Backlog items into multiple smaller Product Backlog items.
Forecasting the effort required of Product Backlog items.
Reducing or ideally eliminating dependencies between items
trap: Product Backlog is 'ordered', not strictly 'prioritized' by a single metric. Additionally, forecasting effort is the responsibility of the Developers, not the Product Owner.
explanation: Correct: Backlog management involves breaking down large items (refinement), collaborating and reviewing items with stakeholders, and structuring items to minimize dependencies.

text: The user satisfaction gap is the difference between … (choose the best two answers)
options: The current market share of the product.
The total market size.
The user's actual experience.
The user's desired experience.
trap: Do not confuse market share metrics with user satisfaction and experience gaps.
explanation: Correct: In EBM, the 'Unrealized Value' is represented by the Satisfaction Gap—the difference between the user's desired experience and their current actual experience.

text: If you are uncertain about customer needs and what the market wants, what should you do? (choose the best two answers)
options: Consider developing a different product.
Spend more time on validating your customer need assumptions.
Release often with smaller releases.
Spend more time creating a risk management plan.
trap: Creating extensive risk management plans is a predictive traditional approach that fails in complex environments.
explanation: Correct: To combat market uncertainty, the Product Owner must validate assumptions quickly and release small increments frequently to obtain real-world user feedback.

text: Why does Agile insist on frequent product releases? (choose the best option)
options: All of the above.
They enable teams to inspect and adapt more frequently.
Smaller, more frequent releases are less risky.
They help teams better understand and meet customer needs.
None of the above.
They help teams to learn how to correct and eliminate errors.
trap: Do not pick a single benefit when all listed benefits are valid reasons for frequent releases.
explanation: Correct: 'All of the above.' Frequent releases drive feedback loops, mitigate deployment risks, validate user needs, and allow continuous learning and course correction.

text: Which statement is the best description of the Sprint Review? (Choose the best answer)
options: A chance to evaluate the Sprint's outcome and decide on future adjustments.
A showcase of the functionality accomplished in the Sprint.
An examination of the work completed by the Developers during the Sprint.
A meeting to retrospectively analyze the team's performance during the Sprint.
A planning session to decide on the scope of work for the next Sprint.
trap: The Sprint Review is not just a demo or showcase. It is a collaborative working session.
explanation: Correct: The Sprint Review is an event to inspect the Sprint's outcome, present progress, and collaboratively decide on future adaptations to the Product Backlog.

text: You are put in a difficult position by the Executive team. Your product is losing paying customers. The CEO believes new features delivered at a quicker rate will bring customers back. The marketing executive thinks the loss of customers is down to a shrinking market and increasing new feature releases will not make much difference at this point. Which action might you take? (choose the best answer)
options: Collaborate with the Executive team to run a small experiment to make an informed decision.
Agree with the CEO and add features to the Product Backlog as it might increase your customer base.
Suggest voting to the stakeholders to decide which options should be considered.
Acknowledge the views of the CEO but decline to add more features to the product.
trap: Do not resolve conflicts with power dynamics (just agreeing with CEO) or voting. Use empirical data instead.
explanation: Correct: Running a small, inexpensive experiment allows the Scrum Team and Executives to gather empirical data to validate whether new features or market shrinkage is driving user behaviors.

text: A new social media app has entered the market and is starting to steal customers away from your company's primary social media product. After studying this competition you realize they release new and useful features quicker than you can and their app store star rating is higher than yours. What is your best course of action? (choose the best option)
options: Improve your time to market and ability to innovate to respond faster.
Decrease your product price to make it more appealing.
Shift your product to a market with less competition.
Enhance your next release with new features to improve current value, retain users and attract new ones.
trap: Adding more features without fixing the systemic capability to release fast will not solve the underlying competitive disadvantage.
explanation: Correct: When competitors out-innovate you, the best strategic move is to improve your capability to deliver value fast (Time-to-Market) and free up capacity for innovation (Ability to Innovate).

text: A new Scrum team has been ineffective at forecasting the effort required for their Sprint Backlog items. Due to items taking longer than predicted, they fear they will not be able to meet the Sprint Goal and inform yourself as the Product Owner. What first action should you take? (choose the best first option)
options: Inform management that more resources are needed.
End the Sprint, since the goal cannot be achieved.
Change the Sprint Goal to match what the Developers can deliver.
Skip Product Backlog refinement activities, to gain more development time in the Sprint.
Try to reduce the scope of the Sprint, if possible, to still meet the Sprint Goal.
trap: Never change the Sprint Goal mid-Sprint, and do not cancel the Sprint unless the goal becomes completely obsolete.
explanation: Correct: If work is different than expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate and reduce the scope of the Sprint Backlog while keeping the Sprint Goal intact.

text: During Sprint Planning the Product Owner insists on a large scope for the Sprint Goal. The Backlog items chosen are getting greater than the Developers believe they can meet in the Sprint. Which actions should be taken? (choose all that apply)
options: Change or remove selected Product Backlog items whilst considering the Sprint Goal.
Do not start the Sprint and take a pause between Sprints to work on backlog refinement.
The Developers ensure that the Product Owner is aware, start the Sprint and monitor progress.
Ask the Developers to work overtime for this Sprint and promise that it will not happen again.
Start the Sprint and recruit additional Developers to help.
trap: Do not force overtime, hire people mid-Sprint (which slows down teams), or cancel Sprint starts.
explanation: Correct: During Sprint Planning, if the work is too high, the Scrum Team must negotiate. The Developers and PO collaborate to adjust the items selected, ensuring the forecast is realistic and achievable.

text: During the Sprint, what will the Product Owner be doing? (choose the best 3)
options: Gathering more information and opinions from stakeholders.
Updating the Sprint burndown chart.
Answer questions from the Developers about items in the current Sprint.
Running the Daily Scrum.
Reordering items in the Product Backlog.
Prioritizing the Developers tasks in the Sprint Backlog.
trap: The Product Owner does not run the Daily Scrum, nor do they manage or prioritize the internal tasks of the Developers.
explanation: Correct: During the Sprint, the PO continuously refines the Product Backlog with stakeholders, answers clarifying questions from Developers, and manages the ordering of upcoming work.

text: Which of the below are true regarding the Product Backlog? (choose the best two answers)
options: All Product Backlog items must be expressed as user stories.
All Product Backlog items must be identified before the first Sprint begins.
Only the Product Owner can place items on the Product Backlog.
The Product Backlog represents the input of all stakeholders and eliminates any need for the Developers to speak to stakeholders.
The Product Backlog is ordered by the Product Owner.
The Product Backlog should be visible to the Scrum Team and stakeholders.
trap: Scrum does not mandate User Stories (any format works), and the backlog is dynamic rather than complete upfront.
explanation: Correct: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog, and the backlog must be transparent and visible to both the Scrum Team and stakeholders.

text: As the Product Owner you monitor and share your product usage dashboard which shows usage rate by feature. The data shows a particular feature is seldom used. An influential stakeholder disputes the data, and insists that the particular feature is essential, despite indicated low usage rates. The stakeholder believes that measuring feature usage is a waste of time, as it is obvious that the feature should be useful. You have confirmed that the data is accurate. What should you do? (choose the best answer)
options: Stop measuring feature usage to please the stakeholder.
Continue measuring feature usage and use it to inform your decisions, but do not publish it.
Remove the feature.
Keep measuring and openly share the data for transparency, and use it for decision-making.
trap: Do not hide data or stop measuring to avoid conflicts. Transparency is a core pillar of Scrum.
explanation: Correct: 'Keep measuring and openly share the data...' Empirical decision-making relies on transparency. Keeping metrics visible allows honest, data-driven conversations rather than opinion-based direction.

text: You release a feature that came from requirements provided to you from a key stakeholder. You find that the feature does not actually get used. You suspect the key stakeholder and other stakeholders do not understand the needs of the users as much as they think. Should you discuss this with them? (choose the correct answer)
options: Yes. They should realise their association with wasted effort.
No. You should show that the feature hasn't been used yet, but suggest it might be used in the future.
No. Look for new users who need this feature.
Yes. If you share what you learned from the release, it may help them improve their understanding and ability to research what users actually need.
trap: Do not turn feedback into blame or try to find excuses for unused work. Use it as a learning opportunity.
explanation: Correct: Sharing empirical usage data with stakeholders helps them refine their understanding of user needs, promoting collaborative hypothesis-testing instead of gut-feeling assumptions.

text: Your organization has recently adopted Scrum. Management want to know which metrics are most useful in assessing how valuable the users find the product. Which two metrics would be most suitable? (choose the best two options)
options: Number of features released per month
Customer satisfaction.
On-time release ratio.
Team velocity.
Frequency of use per feature.
trap: Velocity and feature output measure delivery activities, not the actual realized value delivered to the user.
explanation: Correct: Customer satisfaction and feature usage frequency measure actual realized value and user engagement, which align directly with the 'Current Value' Key Value Area in EBM.

text: How much information is actually needed to start a Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: Enough so the Developers can create a forecast of what they can do during the Sprint.
Just enough to understand the design and architecture.
Just enough tasks for the Scrum Master and Product Owner to be confident in the Developer's understanding of the Sprint.
All of the potential tasks. Sprint Planning cannot finish until all of the work is identified and estimated.
trap: Do not require complete technical designs or exhaustive task breakdowns before starting a Sprint.
explanation: Correct: A Sprint can start as soon as there is enough high-level clarity and selected items for the Developers to confidently forecast their initial work.

text: Who should know the most about the progress toward a business objective or a release?
options: The Product Owner.
The Project Manager.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
trap: Progress toward business objectives is tracked through the Product Backlog — the Product Owner's domain, not a project manager's.
explanation: The best answer is the Product Owner. Because the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing value and manages the Product Backlog - the emergent plan for reaching the Product Goal - they hold the clearest picture of progress toward business objectives and releases. The Developers, Scrum Master, and a project-manager role each have a different or non-existent focus here. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Which are two good ways for the Development Team to ensure security concerns are addressed?
options: Have the Scrum Team create Product Backlog items for security concerns.
Postpone security concerns until the end of the project.
Add security concerns to the Definition of "Done.".
Include a Sprint to specifically resolve all security concerns.
trap: Quality is built in continuously; a dedicated 'security Sprint' or deferring security are classic anti-patterns.
explanation: Security is a quality attribute that must be built in continuously rather than bolted on. Adding security criteria to the Definition of Done ensures every Increment addresses it, and creating Product Backlog items makes specific security work visible and ordered. A one-off 'security Sprint' or postponing security to the end both defer quality and contradict delivering a Done, usable Increment each Sprint. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: At what point should the Sprint Retrospective be held?
options: In the middle of each Sprint.
Solely at the conclusion of the last Sprint of a release.
At the end of each Sprint.
At the beginning of the last Sprint of a release.
trap: The Retrospective happens every Sprint, not only at release milestones.
explanation: The best answer is at the end of each Sprint. The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint, so it happens every Sprint to inspect the work and plan improvements. Confining it to the last Sprint of a release, or holding it mid-Sprint, would remove the regular inspect-and-adapt rhythm. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10 - Sprint Retrospective)

text: Which two things should a Scrum Team do during the first Sprint?
options: Develop at least one piece of functionality.
Create the complete Product Backlog to be developed in subsequent Sprints.
Define the major product features and a release plan architecture.
Develop and deliver at least one piece of functionality.
trap: Even the first Sprint must deliver working functionality — there is no 'Sprint 0' for planning or architecture only.
explanation: Every Sprint, including the first, must produce a usable, valuable Increment - at least one piece of working functionality. The first Sprint is not a planning-only phase: defining all features and a full architecture up front, or trying to complete the entire Product Backlog before development, contradicts empirical, incremental delivery. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: What would "increment" mean in Scrum?
options: A set of tasks.
A potentially releasable piece of working product.
A prototype.
A group of features still in progress.
trap: An Increment is usable working product, not a prototype or a set of unfinished tasks.
explanation: The best answer is that an Increment is a usable, potentially releasable piece of working product that meets the Definition of Done. It is more than a prototype, a set of tasks, or a bundle of features still in progress - it is concrete, verified, and additive to prior Increments. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: What is the primary thing a Product Owner can do?
options: Make certain that all stakeholder needs are met.
Maximize the value delivered by the product.
Determine the release schedule and contents.
Function as the single source of truth for all requirements.
trap: The PO serves value, not stakeholder appeasement — satisfying every stakeholder need is not the goal.
explanation: According to the Scrum Guide, the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, so that is the best answer. Meeting every stakeholder need, owning the release schedule, or acting as the single source of all requirements are narrower or inaccurate framings - value maximization, expressed through ordering and managing the Product Backlog, is the core accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: In what way can a Product Owner foster stakeholder collaboration?
options: Sharing roadmap and progress transparently.
Letting the Scrum Master handle all communication.
Hiding unfinished work to avoid questions.
Organizing frequent reviews with feedback loops.
trap: Transparency builds collaboration; delegating all communication to the Scrum Master isolates the PO.
explanation: Stakeholder collaboration is built on openness. Frequent reviews with feedback loops and transparently sharing the roadmap and progress keep stakeholders engaged and aligned. Hiding unfinished work or routing all communication through the Scrum Master contradicts the Scrum values of openness and respect and weakens the empirical feedback the Product Owner depends on. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: In what way is management external to the Scrum Team involved in the Daily Scrum?
options: The Product Owner represents their opinions.
They are not involved.
Management gives an update on organizational initiatives at the beginning of each Daily Scrum.
The Scrum Master speaks on their behalf.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers only — management has no active part in it.
explanation: The best answer is that external management is not involved in the Daily Scrum - it is a 15-minute event for the Developers. If a Product Owner or Scrum Master is actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they take part as Developers. Management does not give updates, and neither the Product Owner nor Scrum Master attends to represent outside voices. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9 - Daily Scrum)

text: Your product is losing customers, and the stakeholder insists on adding new features. What two actions might you take?
options: Collaborate with the stakeholder to run a small experiment to validate their opinion.
Acknowledge their views but decline to add more features.
Concur with the stakeholder and add features to the Product Backlog as it might increase your customer base.
Collaborate with other stakeholders and use a voting system.
trap: Adding features on demand when customers are leaving treats output as the fix; validate the problem first.
explanation: Empirical product ownership validates opinions with evidence before committing scope. Running a small experiment tests the stakeholder's assumption, and it is legitimate to acknowledge their view yet decline to add features that lack supporting evidence. Simply agreeing to add features, or settling the question with a stakeholder vote, substitutes opinion and politics for data. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: A Development Team selects a set of Product Backlog items for a Sprint Backlog with the intent to get the selected items done by the end of the Sprint. Which three phrases best describe the purpose of a Definition of Done?
options: It defines what it takes for an Increment to be ready for release.
It controls whether the Developers have performed their tasks.
It guides the Development Team in creating a forecast at the Sprint Planning.
It tracks the percentage complete of a Product Backlog item.
It creates transparency over the work inspected at the Sprint Review.
trap: The Definition of Done is not a progress-tracking or performance-control tool.
explanation: The Definition of Done creates transparency about what 'complete' means: it makes the work inspected at the Sprint Review transparent, helps the Developers forecast realistically during Sprint Planning, and defines what it takes for an Increment to be releasable. It is not a percent-complete tracker, nor a mechanism to police individual task performance. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done) Question 11 What actions support frequent delivery? Options & Réponses : ● ● ● ● [ ] Avoiding user feedback. [x] Maintaining a Definition of Done. [ ] Using a sequential waterfall process. [x] Automating deployment. Explication générale : Frequent delivery is enabled by automation and a clear quality bar. Automating deployment shortens the path to release, and a solid Definition of Done keeps every Increment releasable. A sequential waterfall process and ignoring user feedback both work against agility and fast, valuable delivery. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: What practices help align development with strategic goals in Scrum?
options: Backlog ordering by business value.
Refinement focused on Product Goal.
Regular stakeholder reviews.
Avoiding release until everything is done.
trap: Delaying release until 'everything is done' works against strategic alignment and fast feedback.
explanation: Aligning delivery with strategy relies on continuous refinement toward the Product Goal, regular stakeholder reviews, and ordering the backlog by business value. Refusing to release until 'everything' is done contradicts incremental delivery and delays feedback and value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What must an efficient Product Owner do?
options: Be the "expert" opinion for all Product Backlog items.
Be the single point of contact for all stakeholders.
Ensure that the team is as productive as possible.
All of the above.
None of the above.
Make certain that every stakeholder need is met.
trap: A PO who plays expert, gatekeeper and full-time co-locator for everything becomes a bottleneck — none of these define efficiency.
explanation: The best answer is 'none of the above'. Being the sole expert on every item, maximizing raw productivity, satisfying every stakeholder, or being the only point of contact all misframe the role or turn the Product Owner into a bottleneck. Effectiveness comes from maximizing value and empowering the team, not from owning every decision. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What of these options are signs of a strong Product Owner?
options: Prioritizing value over velocity.
Blocking stakeholder access.
Decisions based on user data.
Adjusting backlog based on feedback.
trap: Blocking stakeholder access is a sign of weakness, not strength — strong POs manage engagement, not isolation.
explanation: Strong Product Owners are evidence-driven, value-focused, and responsive. Basing decisions on user data, prioritizing value over raw velocity, and adjusting the backlog from feedback all reflect this. Blocking stakeholder access removes the transparency and collaboration effective ownership depends on. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What does a Product Owner manage?
options: The Product Backlog.
Task assignments.
Team performance.
Product vision alignment.
trap: The PO manages the Product Backlog and vision — never task assignments or team performance.
explanation: The Product Owner manages the Product Backlog and keeps it aligned with the product vision and Product Goal. Team performance and task assignments are not the Product Owner's to manage - the Developers self-manage their work, and no one assigns their tasks. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: Which are good ways for a Product Owner to validate assumptions?
options: Rely only on stakeholder intuition.
Build the feature and wait for user feedback.
Use hypothesis-driven development.
Conduct A/B testing.
trap: Building first and waiting for feedback is not validation — test assumptions before investing.
explanation: Assumptions are best validated with evidence. Hypothesis-driven development and A/B testing produce empirical data quickly and cheaply. Building the full feature first and waiting, or relying on stakeholder intuition, delays learning and risks investing in low-value work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What activities would a Product Owner typically undertake between the end of the current Sprint and the next Sprint Planning?
options: Refining the Product Backlog.
Working with the Quality Assurance departments on the Increment of the current Sprint.
There are no such activities. The next Sprint starts immediately after the current Sprint.
Updating the project plan with the stakeholders.
trap: There is no gap between Sprints — a new Sprint starts immediately when the previous one ends.
explanation: The best answer is that there are no such activities - a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends. There is no gap or phase between Sprints. Necessary work such as Product Backlog refinement happens inside the Sprint, not in a break between Sprints. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: At what point is a Sprint over?
options: When all the tasks are completed.
Once the Product Owner states it is done.
When all Product Backlog items meet their Definition of "Done.".
When the timebox expires.
trap: A Sprint ends when its timebox expires, regardless of whether work is complete.
explanation: The best answer is: when the timebox expires. A Sprint is a fixed-length event of one month or less and ends when its timebox is reached, regardless of whether every item is finished - this is what makes inspection and adaptation happen on a regular cadence. It does not end because the Product Owner declares it, nor because all items meet the Definition of Done or all tasks are complete. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: After launching a premium pricing tier, a Product Owner wants to evaluate whether the new tier delivers value. Which evidence would be most meaningful?
options: Velocity increase during the Sprints that built the feature
Total lines of code deployed for the pricing feature
Increase in customer conversion to the premium tier and reduced churn among premium users
Number of Sprint Backlog items completed to build the tier
trap: Velocity, lines of code and item counts measure output, not the business outcome of a pricing change.
explanation: The best answer is the increase in premium conversion and reduced churn among premium users - outcome metrics that reflect real customer and business value. Sprint Backlog items completed, lines of code deployed, and velocity are output measures that say nothing about whether the new tier actually delivers value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: At what point does a Developer become the sole owner of an item or task on the Sprint Backlog?
options: Never. All Sprint Backlog items are "owned" by the Developers as a whole.
During the Daily Scrum.
Whenever a Developer takes responsibility for it.
During the Sprint Planning event.
trap: No individual ever 'owns' a Sprint Backlog item — the Developers own it collectively.
explanation: The best answer is 'never' - Sprint Backlog items are owned collectively by the Developers. Scrum relies on shared accountability: although an individual may pick up a specific item, the Developers as a whole remain accountable for the Sprint's work and its Increment. Ownership does not transfer at Sprint Planning, at the Daily Scrum, or simply because someone starts working on an item. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Backlog) Voici l'extraction au format texte pour chacune des captures d'écran envoyées :

text: What would be the primary reason the Product Owner must be a single person and not a group or committee?
options: To reduce costs by not hiring multiple roles.
To provide clarity and quick decision-making around product direction.
To make sure someone is available to attend meetings.
To ensure one person writes all the Product Backlog items.
trap: One PO exists for decision clarity and speed, not for cost savings or meeting attendance.
explanation: The best answer is that a single Product Owner provides clarity and enables quick, coherent decisions about product direction. When one person is accountable, the organization knows whose decisions to respect and value is not diluted by committee. It is not about meeting attendance, cost savings, or having one person write every backlog item. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 Product Owner)

text: Which are effective Product Owner decision-making techniques?
options: User research data.
HIPPO-based decision making (Highest Paid Person's Opinion).
Cost of delay analysis.
Consensus-based voting only.
trap: HIPPO (highest paid person's opinion) and pure consensus voting both bypass evidence.
explanation: Effective Product Owner decisions are evidence-driven. Cost-of-delay analysis and real user research data ground decisions in value and outcomes. Deferring to the highest-paid person's opinion (HIPPO) or relying on consensus voting alone substitutes authority or compromise for evidence, which is unreliable in complex work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What would be an important quality of an effective Product Vision?
options: All of the above.
It forms a contract with the business, allowing change to be better managed.
It has the approval of all stakeholders.
It inspires the people who will deliver the product.
trap: A vision that inspires is not a contract — locking scope or requiring universal approval kills its purpose.
explanation: The best answer is that an effective Product Vision inspires the people who will deliver the product. A compelling vision creates focus and commitment - two of the Scrum values. Requiring the sign-off of every stakeholder, or treating the vision as a fixed contract, works against the adaptability Scrum depends on. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: What best explains a Sprint Review?
options: It is a mechanism to control the Developers' activities during a Sprint.
It is a demo at the end of the Sprint for everyone in the organization to check on the work done.
It is when the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of a Sprint and figure out what to do next.
trap: The Sprint Review is a working session to inspect and adapt, not a demo or a control gate.
explanation: The best answer is that the Sprint Review is where the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Sprint's outcome and determine what to do next. It is a working, collaborative session - not a formal demo for the whole organization, and not a mechanism to control the Developers' activities during the Sprint. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review)

text: What statement is true about Sprint Planning?
options: Sprint Planning only involves the Developers.
The Product Owner dictates what will be delivered.
The Developers select what can be done based on capacity and forecast.
The Scrum Master decides team capacity.
trap: The Developers select the work — neither the PO nor the Scrum Master dictates the forecast.
explanation: The best answer is that the Developers select what can be done based on their capacity and forecast. Sprint Planning is collaborative: the Product Owner brings priorities and the Sprint's value, but the Developers decide how much to take on. The Product Owner does not dictate the amount of work, the Scrum Master does not set capacity, and the event involves the whole Scrum Team, not only the Developers. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning)

text: At what point does a Developer become accountable for the value of a Product Backlog item selected for the Sprint?
options: Never. The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating value every Sprint.
At the Sprint Planning Event.
Whenever a Developer has the expertise to contribute to the work.
During the Daily Scrum.
trap: Value accountability sits with the PO and the whole Scrum Team — it never transfers to an individual Developer.
explanation: The best answer is 'never' - the entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint. Value creation is collective, so accountability does not attach to an individual Developer at Sprint Planning, at the Daily Scrum, or when someone has the relevant expertise. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: In what way can a Product Owner ensure value is delivered each Sprint?
options: Define the Definition of Done.
Prioritize the Product Backlog based on value.
Assign work to Developers.
Track individual performance.
trap: The PO orders by value; the Definition of Done and work assignment belong to others.
explanation: The best answer is to prioritize the Product Backlog based on value - ordering items for maximum impact is how the Product Owner drives value each Sprint. Tracking individual performance and assigning work to Developers undermine self-management, and the Definition of Done is owned by the whole Scrum Team, not created by the Product Owner alone. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 Product Owner)

text: What option below activities should a Product Owner never do?
options: Accept work done during the Sprint.
Establish a Product Goal.
Dictate the Sprint Goal.
Decide when to release the product Increment.
trap: The Sprint Goal is crafted collaboratively at Sprint Planning — the PO must never dictate it.
explanation: The best answer is that a Product Owner should never dictate the Sprint Goal. The Sprint Goal is crafted collaboratively by the whole Scrum Team during Sprint Planning; the Product Owner may propose it but cannot impose it. Establishing a Product Goal, accepting work, and deciding when to release are all legitimate Product Owner activities. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: What may weaken empiricism?
options: Frequent inspection.
Ignoring feedback.
Absence of transparency.
Slow adaptation to insights.
trap: Frequent inspection strengthens empiricism — it is the opposite of a weakness.
explanation: Empiricism rests on transparency, inspection, and adaptation. It is weakened when transparency is absent, when feedback from inspection is ignored, or when the team is slow to adapt to what it learns. Frequent inspection is not a weakness - it is one of the three pillars that make empiricism work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: When using Scrum, what are the responsibilities of a Tester in a Development Team?
options: Checking the work of the developers.
There is no specific tester role.
Finding bugs to assure quality.
Everyone in the Development Team is responsible for the quality of the product.
Creating code coverage reports for the test manager.
trap: Scrum has no tester role: quality is a whole-team accountability.
explanation: Scrum defines no separate tester role. The Developers are collectively accountable for quality by adhering to the Definition of Done, so everyone shares responsibility for a quality product even when individuals bring testing skills. Framing testing as one person checking others' work, hunting bugs, or producing coverage reports for a test manager reintroduces the hand-offs Scrum removes. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team) Question 31 Which of these options statements is true about a Product Vision? Options & Réponses : ● ● ● ● [ ] All of the above. [ ] It is the shared responsibility of the Scrum Team to develop and evolve. [ ] It must be completely free from discussions about strategic technology choices. [x] It develops as the Scrum Team learns more about customers and their needs. ● [ ] None of the above. Explication générale : The best answer is that a Product Vision develops as the Scrum Team learns more about customers and their needs - it is emergent, not fixed. It is not a shared accountability equal across the team (the Product Owner leads it), and it is not required to exclude technology considerations. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 Product Goal)

text: What would be the benefit of a shared understanding of "value"?
options: It eliminates all conflicts.
It ensures every stakeholder gets their way.
It removes the need for feedback.
It aligns the team toward delivering meaningful outcomes.
trap: Shared understanding of value aligns; it does not eliminate conflict or feedback.
explanation: The best answer is that a shared understanding of value aligns the team toward delivering meaningful outcomes, even when trade-offs are required. It does not guarantee every stakeholder gets their way, remove the need for feedback, or eliminate all conflict. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: At what point should a Product Owner update the project plan?
options: Scrum forbids having a project plan.
The Product Backlog is the plan in Scrum. It is updated as new information and insights emerge.
Prior to Sprint Planning to know how much work will have to be done in the Sprint.
After the Daily Scrum to ensure an accurate daily overview of project progress.
trap: In Scrum the Product Backlog IS the plan — there is no separate project plan to maintain.
explanation: The best answer is that in Scrum the Product Backlog is the plan, updated continuously as new information and insights emerge. It is the single, emergent source of work and needs no separate project plan tied to Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, or a fixed schedule. Scrum does not forbid plans - the Product Backlog is that living plan. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: Product A: High Current Value, Low Unrealized Value. Product B: Low Current Value, High Unrealized Value. What step should you take?
options: Weight your investment toward Product B.
Weight your investment toward Product A.
Put equal resources into both products.
trap: High Current Value with low Unrealized Value means little upside left — invest where potential remains.
explanation: The best answer is to weight investment toward Product B. High Unrealized Value signals significant future opportunity that has not yet been captured, so investing there supports long-term growth - especially when Product A already carries high Current Value with little remaining upside. Splitting resources equally ignores this asymmetry, and doubling down on the mature Product A chases diminishing returns. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: In what way does the Definition of Done support transparency?
options: By detailing the project plan.
By ensuring consistent quality for all work.
By standardizing team salaries.
By limiting communication.
trap: The DoD creates transparency through consistent quality, not through documentation or plans.
explanation: The best answer is that the Definition of Done supports transparency by ensuring all work meets a common quality standard. When everyone shares the same bar for 'Done', the Increment's true state is visible to the team and stakeholders. It has nothing to do with standardizing salaries, detailing a project plan, or limiting communication. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which statement is true about a Definition of Done?
options: It is created by stakeholders.
It ensures transparency on what "Done" means.
It changes from Sprint to Sprint.
It is optional in Scrum.
trap: The DoD is mandatory and stable enough to create shared understanding — not a stakeholder artifact reset each Sprint.
explanation: The best answer is that the Definition of Done ensures transparency about what 'Done' means, giving the whole team and stakeholders a shared understanding of completeness and quality. It is not re-invented each Sprint on a whim, it is not created by stakeholders, and it is never optional - work that does not meet it cannot be released or shown as Done. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: What would be a main advantage of a well-defined Definition of Done?
options: It enables the team to release when ready.
It permits skipping testing.
It replaces the need for documentation.
It restricts creativity.
trap: A strong DoD enables releasing when ready — it never authorizes skipping quality work.
explanation: The best answer is that a clear Definition of Done lets the team release when ready, because every Increment meets a consistent, releasable quality bar. It does not permit skipping testing, restrict creativity, or replace documentation - it defines the minimum quality an Increment must meet. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which output from Sprint Planning provides the Developers with a target and overarching direction for the Sprint?
options: Sprint Backlog.
The release plan.
The Sprint Goal.
Sprint Review minutes.
trap: The Sprint Goal gives direction; the Sprint Backlog is the plan, not the target.
explanation: The best answer is the Sprint Goal. It is the single objective for the Sprint and provides the overarching direction, creating coherence and focus so the Developers work toward one aim. The Sprint Backlog is the plan of work; review minutes and the release plan are not outputs of Sprint Planning that set the Sprint's direction. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: Which option below measures could help you determine whether your product is delivering value to your customer?
options: All of the above.
The count of "must-do" Product Backlog items delivered in a release.
The on-schedule performance of the Development Team.
How often your customers use your product.
The average cost of your product release.
None of the above.
trap: Schedule adherence and 'must-do' item counts measure output; usage measures value.
explanation: The best answer is how often customers use the product. Actual usage is a direct outcome measure of delivered value, which is what the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing. Counting delivered 'must-do' items, on-schedule performance, and release cost are output or cost measures that do not, by themselves, show whether customers find the product valuable. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: When a Product Owner is too busy to work with all teams in a multi-team environment, which strategy will help?
options: Assign sub-Product Owners to each Scrum Team.
Enlist the Program Management Office.
Communicate a clear Product Goal and delegate some activities to the Developers.
All of the above.
Include component team Product Owners.
trap: Proxy or sub-Product Owners fragment accountability — delegation with a clear Product Goal preserves it.
explanation: The best answer is to communicate a clear Product Goal and delegate some activities to the Developers. There is one Product Owner per product; rather than splitting the role or adding sub-owners and PMO layers, the Product Owner keeps accountability while delegating specific work. A clear Product Goal keeps teams aligned even when the Product Owner cannot be everywhere. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: Who would be required to attend the Daily Scrum?
options: The Scrum Team.
The Developers and Scrum Master.
The Developers and Product Owner.
The Scrum Master and Product Owner.
Developers.
trap: Only the Developers are required; SM and PO attend only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers - the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for them. The Product Owner or Scrum Master attend only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, in which case they participate as Developers. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9 - Daily Scrum)

text: You work as a Product Owner for a small company and your Development Team employee retention rate has been falling. Data from exit interviews suggests that a Development Team members are frustrated by interruptions and low-value meetings and feel that their work is not "meaningful." You need to address this quickly, since the cost to train new Development Team members is very high in a small organization like yours. To increase the likelihood of improving the retention rate, what additional measurements should you consider when determining improvements?
options: All of the above.
Employee Net Promoter Scores.
The Innovation Rate, which is the ratio of new work to total work.
The On-Product Index, the ratio of product work to total work.
trap: Retention is an Ability-to-Innovate concern — several complementary measures apply, not just one.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Innovation Rate, the On-Product Index, and employee Net Promoter Score together show whether Developers are doing meaningful, valuable work and feel engaged - the factors behind the retention problem. No single metric captures all three. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Which statements accurately describe a Product Backlog?
options: Ordered based on priority, value, dependencies, and risk.
Only visible to the Product Owner and stakeholders.
An inventory of things to be done.
Managed by the Product Owner.
An exhaustive list of requirements to be implemented.
trap: The Product Backlog is transparent and emergent — never exhaustive nor private to the PO.
explanation: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of everything needed to improve the product - an inventory of work that the Product Owner manages and orders by value, dependencies, and risk. It is transparent to the whole Scrum Team and stakeholders, not restricted to the Product Owner, and it is never a fixed, exhaustive requirements list. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: In what way can the Product Owner make the Product Backlog more actionable?
options: Ensure clarity and acceptance criteria.
Break down large items.
Estimate items for a full year ahead.
Assign tasks to Developers.
trap: Actionability comes from clarity and small items, not from year-long estimation or task assignment.
explanation: Actionable backlog items are small and clear with agreed acceptance criteria. Breaking down large items and clarifying them makes them ready for delivery. Assigning tasks to Developers or estimating a full year ahead add neither clarity nor agility. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What actions can help improve Time-to-Market in the Scrum environment?
options: Creating a release plan upfront for 12 months.
Reducing batch sizes.
Adding more Developers to a team mid-Sprint.
Continuous delivery practices.
trap: Adding people mid-Sprint or big upfront release plans slow delivery rather than speed it.
explanation: Time-to-Market improves by reducing batch sizes and adopting continuous-delivery practices, which speed feedback and flow. Adding Developers mid-Sprint disrupts the team, and a fixed 12-month release plan is neither empirical nor adaptive. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: When should a Product Increment be released?
options: All planned features for the release are done.
The Increment has met all of its quality goals.
The definition of "Done" has been met.
The Product Owner decides it is ready to be released.
trap: Release timing is the PO's value decision — not an automatic consequence of quality gates or scope completion.
explanation: The best answer is when the Product Owner decides it is ready. Releasing is the Product Owner's call; the Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value, and an Increment may be delivered whenever it provides value. Meeting the Definition of Done makes an Increment releasable, but the timing decision is the Product Owner's. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: You started measuring product feature usage in your last release. You are surprised to learn that a sizable percentage of a features you thought were very important are never or rarely used. Which of these options actions could you take to further evaluate this unexpected result?
options: Disable the features that have never been used and listen for feedback.
Examine whether the rarely used features solve the intended problem.
Run experiments to increase your understanding of what customers find valuable.
Invest more time talking to Users to identify the impact they seek.
trap: When features go unused, the instinct to keep building is the trap — investigate and experiment instead.
explanation: Discovering that important-seeming features go unused is a cue to inspect and adapt empirically: talk to users about the impact they seek, disable unused features and listen, run experiments, and check whether rarely used features actually solve the intended problem. All four deepen understanding of real value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: Which of these options statements about the Product Backlog are true? (select two accurate answers)
options: All Product Backlog items must be expressed as user stories.
The Product Backlog is ordered by the Product Owner.
The Product Backlog should be visible to the Scrum Team and stakeholders.
Only the Product Owner can place items on the Product Backlog.
The Product Backlog represents the input of all stakeholders and eliminates any need for the Developers to speak to stakeholders.
All Product Backlog items must be identified before the first Sprint begins.
trap: User stories are optional technique, not a Scrum rule; anyone can propose items but the PO stays accountable.
explanation: The best answers are that the Product Backlog is visible to the Scrum Team and stakeholders and is ordered by the Product Owner. Items need not be user stories, need not all exist before the first Sprint, and the backlog never removes the need for Developers to talk directly with stakeholders. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: How much of a Sprint Backlog must be defined during the Sprint Planning event?
options: The entire Sprint Backlog must be identified and estimated by the end of Sprint Planning.
Enough so the Developers can forecast what they can complete and create a Sprint Goal.
Just enough to understand design and architectural implications.
Just enough tasks for the Scrum Master to be confident in the Developers' understanding of the Sprint.
trap: Sprint Planning needs enough for a forecast — not a fully decomposed Sprint Backlog.
explanation: The best answer is: enough for the Developers to forecast what they can complete and shape a Sprint Goal. The whole Sprint Backlog need not be identified and estimated up front - Developers elaborate the plan during the Sprint as more is learned. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning) Voici l'extraction au format texte avec la suite continue de la numérotation (de 51 à 60) :

text: Managing a Product Backlog involves which of the following activities?
options: Ordering the Product Backlog.
Reviewing the Product Backlog with stakeholders.
Forecasting the effort of Product Backlog items.
Reducing or eliminating dependencies between Product Backlog items.
Breaking large Product Backlog items into multiple smaller Product Backlog items.
trap: Effort forecasting belongs to the Developers, not to Product Backlog management by the PO.
explanation: Managing the Product Backlog includes reviewing it with stakeholders, reducing dependencies between items, ordering the backlog, and breaking large items into smaller ones. Sizing and estimating effort is done by the Developers who will do the work, not by the Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 Product Backlog)

text: Your product's Current Value is low and your most recent three releases have failed to improve a Current Value, but the Unrealized Value is high. Your product cost ratio is high and time-to-market is long. Which strategy should you pursue?
options: Seek out and eliminate the sources of waste to improve your Product Cost Ratio and Time to Market, building a foundation for future innovation.
Drop the product; since you have not been able to improve customer satisfaction, it is better to focus on some other opportunity.
Focus on identifying and delivering high-value features with the limited capacity you have, trying to win customers and increase revenue.
trap: Dropping the product or chasing 'high-value features' without removing waste ignores the systemic cause.
explanation: The best answer is to eliminate the sources of waste driving the high cost ratio and long time-to-market. Before a team can capture its high Unrealized Value it must be able to deliver, so fixing the delivery system first builds the foundation for growth. Chasing features with a broken delivery capability, or abandoning a product with high potential, both miss this. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Who would be on the Scrum Team?
options: All of the above.
Scrum Master.
Developers.
The Product Owner.
trap: The Scrum Team is PO + SM + Developers — leaving any of them out is the trap.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. The Scrum Team consists of one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and the Developers - a single cohesive unit with no sub-teams or hierarchies. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: A Product Vision and Strategy expressed by a Product Owner help to motivate and inform the Development Team and might describe which of the following?
options: Outlining how people will use the product to achieve outcomes.
Describing how the product compares to competitor products.
Describing who will use the product and what they would like to achieve.
Describing how the product will generate revenue.
trap: A vision motivates by covering users, differentiation and viability — not just one dimension.
explanation: A Product Vision and strategy give the Developers context for the Product Goal. It can describe how people will use the product to achieve outcomes, how it compares to competitors, how it generates revenue, and who the users are and what they want to achieve - all of which clarify what is being built and why. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: How small should the "ready" Product Backlog item be?
options: No bigger than 8 story points.
Small enough for a single team member to complete in a Sprint.
It should fit on a small index card.
No longer than one day.
Small enough to build in 1 Sprint.
trap: 'Ready' is about fitting within one Sprint — not story-point ceilings or index cards.
explanation: The best answer is small enough to be Done within one Sprint - that is the practical test of 'ready'. Fitting an index card, a single-person or single-day limit, or a fixed story-point cap are arbitrary constraints Scrum does not prescribe. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What should the Increment be?
options: It must contain every planned feature before it can be shipped.
It must be usable, and the Product Owner decides when to release it.
It must be released to production at the end of every Sprint.
It is only a prototype until a dedicated release Sprint.
trap: The Increment must be usable every Sprint, but releasing it remains the PO's call.
explanation: The best answer is that the Increment must be usable, and the Product Owner decides when to release it. In order to provide value an Increment must be usable, and releasing is a Product Owner decision - an Increment may even be delivered before the Sprint ends, and the Sprint Review is never a gate to releasing value. It need not ship every Sprint, is not a mere prototype, and need not contain all planned features to be released. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 Increment)

text: In what way does the Product Owner benefit from transparency?
options: Clear data for prioritization.
Ability to manipulate metrics.
Avoiding tough decisions.
Early detection of issues.
trap: Transparency serves better decisions — using it to massage metrics or dodge decisions inverts its purpose.
explanation: Transparency gives the Product Owner reliable data to prioritize and lets problems surface early. It exists to support honest, informed decisions - not to manipulate metrics or avoid hard calls. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Transparency)

text: Who decides how work is performed during the Sprint?
options: Subject matter experts.
Architects.
The Developers.
The Scrum Master.
Development Team managers.
trap: Experts, architects and managers advise — only the Developers decide how work gets done.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers. They are self-managing and internally decide who does what, when, and how to turn selected items into a Done Increment. Architects, the Scrum Master, subject-matter experts, and managers do not direct their work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Developers)

text: In what way does Scrum handle changing requirements?
options: Changes are frozen once a Sprint starts.
Change requests go through a change control board.
The Product Backlog is updated regularly based on learning.
Changes must be approved by management.
trap: Scrum has no change control board: the Product Backlog absorbs change continuously.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Backlog is updated regularly as the team learns. Scrum embraces change through continuous refinement, so requirements are not funneled through a change-control board, frozen at Sprint start, or gated by management approval. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog) Question 61 What would be a common risk if a Product Owner is not empowered? Options & Réponses : ● ● ● ● [ ] Quicker time-to-market. [x] Slow decision-making and reduced product value. [ ] Team independence. [ ] Better budget control. Explication générale : The best answer is slow decision-making and reduced product value. When the organization does not respect the Product Owner's decisions, ordering and prioritization stall and value suffers. An empowered Product Owner enables faster, clearer decisions - the opposite of the other options. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: A Scrum Team has been delivering consistently for six months, but team members report feeling disconnected from the product's purpose. Sprint Goals feel arbitrary. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The Scrum Master is not facilitating enough team-building activities
The Daily Scrum is not being run effectively
The team lacks a compelling Product Vision that connects their work to a meaningful long-term direction
Sprint Retrospectives are not producing enough action items
trap: Blaming facilitation or events misses the deeper issue: disengagement often signals a missing compelling vision.
explanation: The best answer is that the team lacks a compelling vision connecting their work to a meaningful long-term direction. The Product Goal provides that direction as the commitment for the Product Backlog; when it is missing or weak, Sprint Goals feel arbitrary. The Daily Scrum, retrospective output, and team-building are not the root cause here. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: Your executive leadership team believes that your product can achieve higher market share. The Sales Leader is pressing you to reduce a price of the product to attract more customers. The Director of Finance is concerned that reducing the price will merely reduce the product's profitability. What sources of information should you consider when deciding whether to drop the price as the Sales Leader is suggesting?
options: Customer satisfaction.
Company earnings targets.
Market share.
Channel sales approach.
Unmet customer needs.
Competitor pricing.
trap: Internal targets (earnings, channel strategy) don't reveal market potential — look outward.
explanation: A value-based pricing decision draws on evidence about customers and the market: customer satisfaction, market share, unmet customer needs, and competitor pricing all inform whether a price drop would truly increase value. The internal channel sales approach and company earnings targets alone are not sufficient grounds for a value-based decision, since they substitute an internal lens for the broader customer and market picture. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Which activities will a Product Owner likely engage in during a Sprint? (select three accurate answers)
options: Run the Daily Scrum.
Reorder items in the Product Backlog.
Gather information and opinions from stakeholders.
Answer questions from the Developers about items in the current Sprint.
Prioritize the Developer's tasks.
Update the Sprint burndown chart.
trap: Running the Daily Scrum or managing Developer tasks are never PO activities.
explanation: During a Sprint the Product Owner stays engaged: gathering stakeholder input, reordering the Product Backlog as insights emerge, and answering the Developers' questions about current items. Prioritizing Developers' tasks, updating the burndown, and running the Daily Scrum belong to the self-managing Developers. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: A Product Owner's team has the highest velocity in the organization, yet the product's market share is declining. What does this suggest about the Product Owner's focus?
options: The Developers should slow down to improve quality
The Scrum Master should take over product decisions to fix the market decline
The Product Owner may be optimizing for output rather than for customer value and market outcomes
The Product Owner should celebrate high velocity as a sign of team excellence
trap: High velocity is output; mistaking it for value delivery is the classic outcome-vs-output trap.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Owner may be optimizing for output rather than customer value and market outcomes. High velocity with falling market share is a classic output-over-outcome signal. Celebrating velocity, handing product decisions to the Scrum Master, or telling Developers to slow down all miss the real issue. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: As Product Owner, you face conflicting stakeholder opinions about a major feature. What is the correct way to you proceed?
options: Rely on the Director of Marketing's opinion and add the features; when revenues increase, you will be vindicated.
Devise an experiment that will help the company to better understand the new market.
Better understand the positions of other stakeholders to gather more information, then make a decision.
Trust the CEO's opinion and focus on current customers.
trap: Deferring to the loudest or most senior voice (CEO, marketing) bypasses evidence-gathering.
explanation: The best answer is to better understand the other stakeholders' positions, gather more information, and then decide. Effective Product Ownership means making an informed, value-based call rather than deferring to the loudest or most senior voice - or jumping straight to an experiment before understanding the problem. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Is this statement correct: Cross-functional teams are optimized to work on one technical layer of the system only.
options: False.
Correct.
trap: Cross-functional teams span all skills to deliver value — single-layer teams are component teams.
explanation: The best answer is False. Cross-functional means the Developers have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint - working across every layer needed to deliver a complete Increment, not optimizing for a single technical layer. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: The Product Owner makes sure the accurate stakeholders are invited to the Sprint Retrospective. They ask the stakeholders not to interrupt and to remain silent during the retrospective.
options: This is not acceptable. Sprint Retrospectives are only for the Scrum Team.
This is acceptable, as the Product Owner is accountable for the Scrum Team interfacing with stakeholders.
trap: The Sprint Retrospective is private to the Scrum Team — stakeholders are not invited.
explanation: The best answer is that this is not acceptable - the Sprint Retrospective is for the Scrum Team only. It is an internal event where the team inspects how the last Sprint went, so inviting stakeholders and asking them to stay silent misunderstands the event's purpose. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10 - Sprint Retrospective)

text: When should an organization reduce its investment in a product?
options: Unrealized Value is very small.
Current Value is very low.
Current Value is very high.
None of the above.
Unrealized Value is very large.
trap: Low Current Value calls for improvement, not divestment; it's low Unrealized Value that signals reduced investment.
explanation: The best answer is when Unrealized Value is very small. Low Unrealized Value means little remaining opportunity, so heavy continued investment yields diminishing returns. Current Value being high or low, on its own, does not signal that further investment has run out of runway. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: The Developers have struggled to get all of their forecasted work done during the last three Sprints. As a Product Owner what steps could you take to help the Developers improve their ability to deliver a Done Increment?
options: Add more people to the team so they can get more done.
Make certain that all Developers are top performers.
Ask the Scrum Master to help the Developers learn techniques for improving their ability to forecast work.
The Product Owner can spend more time with the Developers.
trap: Adding people or ranking performers undermines self-management — improve the system instead.
explanation: The Product Owner can help by collaborating more closely so Developers understand the value and context of the work, and by asking the Scrum Master to coach them on forecasting techniques. Insisting on 'top performers' or simply adding people is neither sustainable nor effective. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 Developers) Question 71 Midway through a Sprint, the Product Owner learns that a competitor just launched a feature that directly threatens the product's market position. The current Sprint Backlog does not address this. What should the Product Owner do? Options & Réponses : ● [ ] Ask the Developers to add competitive response items to the current Sprint Backlog ● [ ] Ignore competitor moves and trust the existing product strategy ● [ ] Cancel the Sprint immediately and start planning a response ● [x] Update the Product Backlog ordering to reflect the new competitive reality for upcoming Sprints Explication générale : The best answer is to update the Product Backlog ordering to reflect the new competitive reality for upcoming Sprints. The current Sprint's Goal and Backlog are protected, so the Product Owner does not inject new work mid-Sprint or cancel the Sprint over a single competitive move - cancelling is reserved for when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Ignoring the competitor would not be empirical. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: If quality assurance work does not occur as part of the development work within a Sprint, which of the following statements are accurate?
options: The Product Owner may still decide to release the product.
The next Sprint may be interrupted when quality issues are encountered.
The visibility of progress on the Product Backlog is not transparent.
The project manager cannot effectively update the plan.
trap: Undone quality work doesn't block a PO's release decision, but it destroys transparency and interrupts later Sprints.
explanation: When quality work is deferred, transparency about what is truly Done is lost, technical debt accumulates, and later Sprints get disrupted by rework.
