The Product Owner still holds release authority. The 'project manager cannot update the plan' option is a distractor - Scrum has no project-manager role. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which two measurements best indicate to the Product Owner that value is being delivered?
options: On-time release trends.
Frequency of feature use.
Scope implemented.
Velocity.
Customer satisfaction.
trap: Velocity, scope and on-time trends measure delivery mechanics, not delivered value.
explanation: Value shows up in outcomes, not outputs. How often features are used and how satisfied customers are reflect delivered value directly. Velocity, on-time release trends, and scope implemented measure activity or output, not whether customers actually received value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: You work as the Product Owner for a small company and your Scrum Team's employee retention rate has been falling. Exit interviews show Developers feel frustrated by interruptions and low-value meetings, and that their work isn't meaningful. What additional measurements should you consider to improve retention?
options: The On-Product Index, the ratio of product work to total work.
The Innovation Rate, which is the ratio of new work to total work.
Employee Net Promoter Scores.
All of the above.
trap: A single metric rarely explains retention issues — EBM combines several Ability-to-Innovate measures.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Innovation Rate and the On-Product Index reveal how much effort goes into valuable product work, and employee Net Promoter Score signals engagement - together they help diagnose why meaningful work and retention are slipping. No single metric captures all three. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: In the scaled environment, how is product alignment best maintained?
options: By using a program manager.
By possessing one centralized Product Owner per team.
By having a shared Product Goal across teams.
By assigning all backlog items centrally.
trap: Alignment at scale comes from a shared Product Goal, not from a coordinating manager layer.
explanation: The best answer is a shared Product Goal across teams. Multiple Scrum Teams on one product share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner, which keeps them aligned. One Product Owner per team, a program manager, or centrally assigned items each fragment ownership or reduce self-management. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: Who would be accountable for maintaining and communicating the Product Goal?
options: All of the above.
Executive Sponsors.
The Product Owner.
The Developers.
Stakeholders.
trap: The Product Goal has exactly one steward: the Product Owner.
explanation: The best answer is the Product Owner, who develops and explicitly communicates the Product Goal and keeps it transparent and understood. Developers, executive sponsors, and stakeholders contribute, but accountability for the Product Goal rests with the Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 Product Goal)

text: A fundamental first step in product ownership is determining what your actual product is. Which option below would probably be the least effective way to enhance the agility of your future product development?
options: Start with a holistic view of how the customer sees your product.
Clearly understand the producer, buyer/consumer relationship.
Lean on your organizational efficiency and existing architecture to build your product aligned to the current organization.
Evaluate whether there is a significantly large enough market for your product.
trap: Starting from internal architecture and efficiency is inside-out thinking — product definition starts with the customer.
explanation: The best answer is anchoring the product to existing organizational efficiency and architecture - this is the least effective way to increase agility. Scrum emphasizes customer value and empiricism, so building around organizational convenience limits adaptability. Assessing market size, understanding the producer-consumer relationship, and taking the customer's holistic view all support agility. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What is the most suitable way for a Product Owner to handle dependencies between teams?
options: Let teams negotiate them during the Sprint.
Identify and minimize dependencies proactively.
Rely on the Scrum Master to resolve them.
Ignore them to promote autonomy.
trap: Ignoring dependencies 'for autonomy' or outsourcing them to the SM lets risk accumulate.
explanation: The best answer is to identify and minimize dependencies proactively, which enables smoother flow and faster delivery. Ignoring them for the sake of autonomy, offloading them to the Scrum Master, or leaving teams to negotiate them mid-Sprint all add risk and delay. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What would be the Scrum Team accountable for?
options: Creating valuable, useful increments every Sprint.
Maximizing stakeholder happiness.
Delivering features exactly as requested.
Writing perfect documentation.
trap: The Scrum Team is accountable for a valuable Increment — not for stakeholder happiness or exact feature compliance.
explanation: According to the Scrum Guide, the entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint. Maximizing stakeholder happiness, producing perfect documentation, or delivering features exactly as requested are secondary to delivering value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: Which best describes a Product Owner's accountability?
options: Creating project plans.
Assigning tasks to Developers.
Maximizing product value.
Writing all user stories.
trap: The PO maximizes value — plans, task assignment and story-writing are means or someone else's work.
explanation: According to the Scrum Guide, the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. Writing every user story, producing project plans, or assigning tasks to Developers are not the Product Owner's accountability - the Developers self-manage their work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: You have more ideas for new products than you have money to invest. What is the suggested approach?
options: Rank proposals by market potential (Unrealized Value) and fully fund as many as you can.
Invest in all of them, but at proportionally lowered amounts, and see how they all perform.
Invest in the proposals that have the highest projected Current Value for the next year.
Finance small experiments to test the proposed ideas and assumptions, then evaluate results.
trap: Ranking on unvalidated potential or spreading money everywhere skips the cheap learning step: small experiments.
explanation: The best answer is to finance small experiments that test the ideas and assumptions, then evaluate the results. With more ideas than money, validating cheaply before committing reduces risk far better than betting on projected value, fully funding by ranked potential, or thinly spreading money across everything. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What techniques support hypothesis-driven development in Scrum?
options: Lean UX.
Feature factories.
Roadmapping.
Impact mapping.
trap: Feature factories and fixed roadmaps are the opposite of hypothesis-driven work.
explanation: Impact mapping and Lean UX support hypothesis-driven development by validating assumptions through experimentation. Roadmapping and 'feature factories' are less empirical - the latter emphasizes output over validated outcomes. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: You find that many features would be never or rarely used. What can you do?
options: Disable the features and listen for feedback.
Invest more time talking to users.
Run experiments to understand customer value.
Examine whether features solve the intended problem.
trap: Doubling down on unused features is the trap — disable, learn, and talk to users instead.
explanation: When features turn out to be rarely used, all of these actions help: talking to users about the impact they seek, disabling unused features and listening for feedback, running experiments, and checking whether the features solve the intended problem. Each supports empirical, value-based decisions. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What would "Done" mean in Scrum?
options: The item is implemented and tested.
The item satisfies the Definition of Done.
The item is documented.
The item meets the Scrum Master's expectations.
trap: 'Done' means meeting the Definition of Done — 'implemented and tested' may still fall short of it.
explanation: The best answer is that an item is 'Done' when it satisfies the Definition of Done - a shared quality standard for the Scrum Team. Being merely implemented and tested, meeting the Scrum Master's expectations, or being documented does not by itself make it Done. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: What makes Product Goals effective in Scrum?
options: Clear and measurable.
Coordinated with stakeholder demands.
Defined by the Scrum Master.
Outcome-oriented.
trap: Effective Product Goals are outcome-driven — not stakeholder wish-lists nor Scrum Master artifacts.
explanation: Effective Product Goals are outcome-oriented and clear and measurable, giving the team meaningful direction. They are not driven by coordinating every stakeholder demand, and they are not defined by the Scrum Master - the Product Owner is accountable for the Product Goal. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 Product Goal)

text: A Scrum Team's Sprint ends on Friday. The Scrum Master proposes holding the Sprint Retrospective on Monday morning to give the team a weekend to reflect. Is this appropriate?
options: Yes — as long as the Product Owner agrees to the delay
No — the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint and must occur within the Sprint timebox, before the next Sprint begins
Yes — rested minds produce better insights
No — but only because the next Sprint starts on Monday
trap: The Retrospective must end within the Sprint's timebox — convenience never moves it into the next Sprint.
explanation: The best answer is no - the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint and must occur within its timebox, before the next Sprint begins. Since a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one, holding it on Monday would push it into the next Sprint. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10 - Sprint Retrospective)

text: What would the Definition of Done be used for?
options: Enhance transparency.
Describe the work that must be done before the Sprint can be declared complete.
Guide the Development Team on how many Product Backlog items to select in a Sprint.
Describe the purpose, objective, and time-box of each Scrum event.
Create a shared understanding of when work is complete.
trap: The DoD defines completeness of work — not event purposes or pre-planning gates.
explanation: The Definition of Done enhances transparency, creates a shared understanding of when work is complete, and helps the Developers judge how much to select in a Sprint. It does not describe event timeboxes, nor is it a checklist of work needed before the Sprint can be 'declared complete'. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which option best describes the Sprint Goal?
options: It is the timeline for completing work.
It serves as the business case for the product.
It is a commitment by the Developers to complete all items.
It is the single objective of the Sprint.
trap: The Sprint Goal is a single objective and a commitment — not a timeline or a business case.
explanation: The best answer is that the Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint. It gives the Developers focus and coherence. It is not the product business case, a promise to complete every selected item, or the Sprint's timeline. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: What should be done if a Sprint Goal becomes obsolete mid-Sprint?
options: The Scrum Master cancels the Sprint.
The Product Owner cancels the Sprint.
The team ignores the issue until the Review.
The Developers revise the Goal.
trap: Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint — not the SM, and Developers cannot rewrite the Goal alone.
explanation: The best answer is that only the Product Owner cancels the Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. The Scrum Master does not cancel it, the Developers do not revise the Goal mid-Sprint, and the issue should not be left until the Review. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: Which outcomes indicate successful Product Ownership in Scrum?
options: Perfectly matching timelines.
Continuous delivery of valuable increments.
Meeting every planned scope item.
High customer satisfaction.
trap: Hitting timelines and full scope are project metrics — Scrum success is measured in value.
explanation: Successful Product Ownership shows up as high customer satisfaction and continuous delivery of valuable increments - outcome measures. Meeting every planned scope item or perfectly matching timelines are output/plan-adherence measures that do not guarantee value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Who holds the final decision about the order of items in the Product Backlog?
options: The Developers.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
Stakeholders.
The CEO.
trap: Stakeholders and the CEO influence, the Developers advise — but the PO alone orders the Product Backlog.
explanation: The best answer is the Product Owner, who is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog. Others may provide input, but the ordering decision - and the accountability for it - rests with the one Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: Which does the self-managing Development Team choose?
options: How to optimally accomplish its work.
When to release, based on its progress.
Sprint length.
Product Backlog ordering.
trap: Self-management covers HOW work is done — not release decisions, Sprint length or backlog ordering.
explanation: The best answer is how to optimally accomplish its work - self-managing Developers decide who does what, when, and how. Sprint length, Product Backlog ordering, and release timing are decided at the Scrum Team or Product Owner level, not by the Developers alone. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 Developers)

text: What would a healthy Product Backlog look like?
options: High-value items are prioritized.
Items are specified out for six months in advance.
Items are refined just-in-time.
All items are estimated in story points.
trap: A backlog fully specified months ahead or 100% estimated is a sign of waterfall thinking, not health.
explanation: A healthy Product Backlog has items refined just-in-time and high-value items ordered first. Detailing items six months out reduces adaptability, and estimating everything in story points is optional - Scrum does not require a specific estimation technique. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: Your stakeholders each have a feature they say is essential for the next release. All are valid. What is the suggested approach?
options: Wait until all essential features are complete before releasing the product.
Escalate to the steering committee to make the call.
Release when you can satisfy at least a single outcome, even though not all features are implemented.
Select the two most influential stakeholders and satisfy their needs, then release.
trap: Waiting for every 'essential' feature or escalating the decision defers value — release on one satisfied outcome.
explanation: The best answer is to release once you can satisfy at least one valuable outcome, even if not every feature is done. Scrum favors early, incremental delivery: shipping a usable outcome and gathering feedback beats delaying for full completion, satisfying only the most influential stakeholders, or escalating the decision. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: What of these options tools support empiricism?
options: Phase gates.
Sprint Reviews.
Gantt charts.
Product usage analytics.
trap: Phase gates and Gantt charts belong to predictive planning, not empiricism.
explanation: Sprint Reviews and product usage analytics support empiricism because they enable inspection and adaptation on real results. Gantt charts and phase gates are predictive, up-front controls that do not provide empirical feedback. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What would be the purpose of the Sprint Review?
options: To present burn-down charts to management.
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and adapt the Product Backlog.
To reassign team responsibilities.
To demonstrate completed work for approval.
trap: The Review is not a status report to management nor an approval gate.
explanation: The best answer is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and adapt the Product Backlog based on stakeholder feedback. The Sprint Review is a collaborative working session, not an approval gate, a status report to management, or a reassignment meeting. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review)

text: If the Product Owner has more work than they can manage, what strategy can help them succeed?
options: Divide the product into components, each with their own Product Owner, and create a Chief Product Owner.
None of the above.
Split the Product Owner role into "Business" and "Technical" Product Owners.
Delegate tasks like detailing Product Backlog items, interviewing users, and analyzing data to Developers.
All of the above.
trap: Splitting the PO role or creating component POs fragments accountability — delegate tasks, keep the accountability.
explanation: The best answer is to delegate tasks such as detailing Product Backlog items, interviewing users, and analyzing data to the Developers. There is still one Product Owner; splitting the role into business/technical owners or components with a 'Chief PO' breaks Scrum's single-owner accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: If burndown charts would be used to visualize progress, what do they track?
options: Individual worker productivity.
Cumulative business value delivered to the customer.
Work remaining across time.
Accumulated cost.
trap: Burndowns track remaining work — not productivity, cost or value.
explanation: The best answer is that a burndown chart tracks work remaining over time. It helps visualize progress toward completion but does not measure business value delivered, accumulated cost, or individual productivity. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: What would be the primary way that a Scrum Master keeps a Development Team working at its highest level of productivity?
options: By removing impediments that hinder the Development Team.
By keeping high value features high in the Product Backlog.
By ensuring the meetings start and end at the proper time.
By facilitating Development Team decisions.
trap: The SM serves the team chiefly by removing impediments — timekeeping and facilitation are secondary.
explanation: The best answer is removing impediments to the Development Team's progress. That is how the Scrum Master helps the team stay effective. Facilitating decisions, timekeeping, and ordering the backlog are either the team's or the Product Owner's responsibility, not the primary productivity lever. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 6-7 - Scrum Master) Voici l'extraction au format texte avec la suite continue de la numérotation (de 101 à 110) :

text: What would be the purpose of a Sprint Review?
options: To inspect the product Increment with stakeholders and collect feedback on next steps.
To review the Scrum Team's activities and processes during the Sprint.
To allocate time to judge the validity of the project.
To build team spirit.
trap: The Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders — it is not a team performance evaluation.
explanation: The best answer is to inspect the Increment with stakeholders and collect feedback on next steps. The Sprint Review exists to inspect outcomes and determine future adaptations - not to judge the project's validity, build team spirit, or review the team's internal processes. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review)

text: What would drawing a trend line through a release burndown chart indicate?
options: When remaining work will likely be completed if nothing changes on the Product Backlog or the Development Team.
The evolution of the cost of the project.
When all Sprint Backlog work will be completed and the Scrum Team will be released for other work.
When the project will be over if the Product Owner removes work that is equal in effort to any new work that is added.
trap: A trend line projects work completion — it says nothing about cost evolution.
explanation: The best answer is that a trend line forecasts when the remaining work will likely be completed if nothing changes on the Product Backlog or in the Development Team. It is a forecast, not a guarantee - and in complex work only what has already happened can inform forward-looking decisions. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: Which are benefits of releasing to users frequently?
options: Delayed ROI.
Increased documentation effort.
Reduced risk of building the wrong thing.
Quicker feedback cycles.
trap: Frequent releases accelerate ROI and learning — 'delayed ROI' is the reverse of reality.
explanation: Releasing to users frequently produces quicker feedback cycles and reduces the risk of building the wrong thing, because assumptions are validated sooner. It does not increase documentation effort or delay ROI - if anything, it accelerates value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: You are the Product Owner for a product with conflicting stakeholder opinions. The CEO says the final decision is yours. What step should you take?
options: Devise an experiment that will help the company to better understand the new market and its potential.
Trust the CEO's opinion and focus on current customers, since you cannot afford unhappy customers.
More fully comprehend the positions of other stakeholders to gather more information, then make a decision.
Trust the Director of Marketing's opinion and add the features; when revenues increase, you will be vindicated.
trap: Siding with the highest authority (CEO) short-circuits understanding the full stakeholder picture.
explanation: The best answer is to more fully understand the other stakeholders' positions, gather information, and then decide. Good Product Ownership balances perspectives and makes an informed, value-based call rather than trusting one opinion or running an experiment before understanding the problem. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Near the end of a Sprint, the team realizes one Product Backlog item meets the acceptance criteria but does not meet the Definition of Done because automated tests are missing. A stakeholder wants it released immediately. What should happen?
options: Present it at Sprint Review as a completed item since acceptance criteria are met
Do not include it in the Increment — it returns to the Product Backlog because it does not meet the Definition of Done
Release it with a note to add tests later, since the stakeholder approved it
Lower the Definition of Done to match what was completed
trap: Acceptance criteria are not the Definition of Done — an item failing the DoD is not part of the Increment.
explanation: The best answer is not to include the item - because the automated tests are missing, it does not meet the Definition of Done, so it is not released and not presented as Done; it returns to the Product Backlog. The Definition of Done is never lowered to match incomplete work, and a stakeholder's approval cannot override it. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which are core elements of Evidence-Based Management?
options: Time-to-Market.
Unrealized Value.
Current Value.
Sprint Velocity.
trap: Sprint velocity is an internal team measure, not an EBM key value area.
explanation: The core Evidence-Based Management measures here are Unrealized Value, Current Value, and Time-to-Market. Sprint velocity is a local team metric, not a business-value indicator, so it is not an EBM Key Value Area. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: A "cone of uncertainty" can be used to do what in Scrum?
options: Represent the relative level of difficulty for predicting the velocity of individual team members.
Determine whether to cut quality, similar to the "Iron Triangle" of project management.
Rapidly identify and prioritize all uncertainties.
Visualize the uncertainty of the potential value that a Scrum Team delivers over time.
trap: The cone visualizes uncertainty of value/forecasts — it is not an effort-scoring or scope-cutting device.
explanation: The best answer is that the cone of uncertainty visualizes the uncertainty of the potential value a Scrum Team delivers over time. It shows how prediction accuracy improves as more is learned - it is not about prioritizing all uncertainties, individual velocity, or trading off quality. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Who bears accountability for maximizing the value of the product?
options: Product Owner.
Stakeholders.
Scrum Master.
Product Manager.
trap: Value accountability belongs to the Product Owner — 'Product Manager' is not a Scrum accountability.
explanation: The best answer is the Product Owner, who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. Stakeholders, the Scrum Master, and a 'product manager' role do not hold this accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: As a Sprint Planning meeting progresses, the Developers realize that the workload is greater than they can handle. Which two are valid actions?
options: The Developers ensure that the Product Owner is aware, start the Sprint, and monitor progress.
The Developers work overtime during this Sprint.
Remove or change selected Product Backlog items.
Hire additional Developers before the end of the Sprint.
Cancel the Sprint.
trap: Working overtime, adding staff or cancelling the Sprint are escalations — renegotiating scope with the PO is the Scrum answer.
explanation: The best answer is that the Developers make sure the Product Owner is aware, start the Sprint, and monitor progress, and that they remove or change selected Product Backlog items. Hiring people, cancelling the Sprint, or planning overtime are not appropriate responses to a large forecast. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 Sprint Planning)

text: What role does a Scrum Master play in supporting product value?
options: They maximize Product Owner's authority.
They coach the team on Scrum and value delivery.
They help the team ship more features.
They write the Product Backlog.
trap: The SM coaches toward value — shipping more features or amplifying PO authority is not the service.
explanation: The best answer is that the Scrum Master coaches the team on Scrum and value delivery. They serve the team and Product Owner rather than maximizing anyone's authority, pushing raw feature output, or writing the Product Backlog. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 6-7 - Scrum Master)

text: Which items would be typically part of Product Backlog refinement?
options: Reordering items based on new info.
Estimating items.
Dividing large PBIs.
Rewriting the Definition of Done.
trap: Refinement never rewrites the Definition of Done — that evolves via the Retrospective.
explanation: Product Backlog refinement typically includes dividing large items, estimating items, and reordering them as new information arrives. Rewriting the Definition of Done is a separate, team-level activity (usually in the Retrospective), not part of routine refinement. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: At what point should a Product Owner adjust a Product Backlog?
options: Only during Sprint Review.
As often as needed to maximize value.
Only when asked by management.
Once per release cycle.
trap: The backlog is adjusted whenever value demands it — not on a management or ceremony calendar.
explanation: The best answer is: as often as needed to maximize value. The Product Owner continuously refines and reorders the Product Backlog based on learning and new opportunities - not only at the Sprint Review, on management request, or once per release. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What happens to undone work at the end of the Sprint?
options: It is automatically released.
It gets included in the Increment.
It is discarded.
It is returned to the Product Backlog.
trap: Undone work is neither released nor discarded — it returns to the Product Backlog for reordering.
explanation: The best answer is that undone work returns to the Product Backlog. Only work meeting the Definition of Done is part of the Increment, so incomplete items are not included, discarded, or released - they go back for future consideration. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What should every Development Team have?
options: At least one representative from each major software engineering discipline.
The competencies and skills needed to deliver a Done Increment without dependencies on others not part of the team.
One lead Developer and no more than 8 other Developers.
trap: Cross-functionality means having all needed skills collectively — not one specialist per discipline.
explanation: The best answer is that every Development Team must have the competencies and skills to deliver a Done Increment without depending on people outside the team. Cross-functionality is about outcomes, not about one representative per discipline or a fixed lead-plus-eight structure. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: What are valid Product Owner activities?
options: Approving code changes.
Defining and ordering Product Backlog items.
Facilitating Sprint Planning.
Monitoring customer satisfaction.
trap: Facilitating events and approving code are not PO work — value and backlog are.
explanation: Defining and ordering Product Backlog items and monitoring customer satisfaction are valid Product Owner activities focused on value. Facilitating Sprint Planning and approving code changes are not the Product Owner's role the event is a whole-team collaboration and the Developers own technical decisions. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Who decides when it is appropriate to update the Sprint Backlog during a Sprint?
options: Project Manager.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
The Product Owner.
trap: The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers; they alone update it during the Sprint.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers. The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers, and they update it throughout the Sprint as more is learned. No project manager, Scrum Master, or Product Owner controls those updates. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Backlog)

text: Which are some responsibilities the Product Owner may share with Developers?
options: Assigning tasks during the Sprint.
Polishing Product Backlog items.
Managing team compensation.
Defining Sprint Goals.
trap: The PO may share refinement work, but never task assignment or HR matters.
explanation: The Product Owner may share activities such as refining Product Backlog items and collaborating on Sprint Goals with the Developers. Managing compensation and assigning tasks during the Sprint fall outside the Scrum Team's accountabilities and are not the Product Owner's to hand over. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: During a Sprint Retrospective, for what is a Scrum Master responsible?
options: Summarizing and reporting the discussions to management.
Participating as a Scrum Team member and facilitating as requested or needed.
Acting as a scribe to capture the Development Team's answers.
Prioritizing the resulting action items.
trap: The SM participates as a peer and facilitates if needed — not as scribe, reporter, or action-item prioritizer.
explanation: The best answer is that the Scrum Master participates as a Scrum Team member and facilitates as requested or needed, keeping the Retrospective positive, productive, and within its timebox. They do not report discussions to management, prioritize the action items, or act as a scribe. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 6-7 - Scrum Master)

text: For what reason is empiricism important in product development?
options: It guarantees perfect predictability.
It permits detailed planning upfront.
It enables learning through inspection and adaptation.
It helps reduce budget variance.
trap: Empiricism enables learning — it never promises predictability or upfront certainty.
explanation: The best answer is that empiricism enables learning through inspection and adaptation. Scrum controls risk in complex work by observing real results and adapting, rather than reducing budget variance, front-loading detailed plans, or promising perfect predictability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: For what reason is early feedback important?
options: It guarantees successful deployment.
It replaces refinement.
It allows quicker value validation.
It decreases stakeholder involvement.
trap: Early feedback validates value — it complements refinement, it doesn't replace it.
explanation: The best answer is that early feedback allows quicker validation of value. Learning sooner lets the team confirm or correct direction, which reduces risk. It does not decrease stakeholder involvement, guarantee deployment, or replace refinement. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: As an investor or shareholder, which of the following measures might give insight about whether a product is delivering value?
options: Revenue per Employee.
The weekly velocity of the Developers.
Product profitability.
Market Share.
The average selling price compared to competitors.
trap: Team velocity means nothing to an investor — business measures like profitability and market share do.
explanation: Investor-facing value shows in outcome and business measures: revenue per employee, market share, average selling price versus competitors, and product profitability. The Developers' weekly velocity is a local activity metric, not a direct value indicator. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What is the proper way for a Product Owner to handle conflicting stakeholder opinions?
options: Let the Developers decide.
Choose the most powerful stakeholder's view.
Avoid the conflict and proceed as before.
Make decisions based on evidence and product goals.
trap: Picking the most powerful stakeholder's view is the classic pressure trap — evidence decides.
explanation: The best answer is to make decisions based on evidence and product goals. The Product Owner resolves conflicting opinions with data and strategy - not by siding with the most powerful stakeholder, handing the decision to the Developers, or avoiding it. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: A Scrum Team has been working on a product for nine Sprints. A new Product Owner comes in, understanding he is accountable for a Product Backlog. However, he is unsure about his responsibilities. Which two activities are part of the Product Owner role?
options: Ensuring that the most valuable functionality is produced first.
Providing the Development Team with detailed specifications.
Creating detailed functional test cases.
Describing features as Use Cases.
Interacting with stakeholders.
trap: A new PO adds value through ordering and stakeholders — not by writing specs or test cases for the team.
explanation: A Product Owner ensures the most valuable functionality is produced first and interacts with stakeholders. Providing detailed specifications, writing features strictly as use cases, and creating detailed test cases are not the Product Owner's accountabilities. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: When might the Sprint be cancelled?
options: When the Developers determine they cannot complete the work.
When sales indicate that there is insufficient money to continue development.
When the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
When it no longer makes sense given the organization's circumstances.
trap: Developers struggling with the forecast is normal variation — only an obsolete Sprint Goal justifies cancellation, by the PO.
explanation: A Sprint may be cancelled when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete or when it no longer makes sense given the organization's circumstances, and only the Product Owner has that authority. Insufficient funds framing, the Developers deciding they cannot finish, or simple difficulty are not cancellation triggers. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: Which are potential signs of low Current Value in EBM?
options: Long time between releases.
High customer churn.
Low Net Promoter Score (NPS).
High product usage.
trap: High usage signals healthy Current Value; long release gaps concern Time-to-Market, not Current Value.
explanation: High customer churn and a low Net Promoter Score point to low Current Value, signaling dissatisfaction. High product usage indicates high value, and time between releases relates more to Time-to-Market than to Current Value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: For what reason is it important to keep Product Backlog items small and clear?
options: It ensures the Product Goal never changes.
It makes planning and delivery easier.
It reduces the number of items in the backlog.
It allows the Scrum Master to assign them.
trap: Small clear items ease planning — they don't freeze the Product Goal or enable task assignment.
explanation: The best answer is that small, clear Product Backlog items make planning and delivery easier. They increase transparency and support confident forecasting not so the Scrum Master can assign them, to shrink the backlog count, or to freeze the Product Goal. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: When determining the ordering of an item on the Product Backlog, what are some things a Product Owner should consider?
options: Importance to customers.
The techniques the Development Team will use to implement it.
Risk.
Alignment and dependencies with existing Product Backlog items.
Alignment with business strategy and goals.
trap: Implementation techniques don't drive ordering — value, risk, dependencies and strategy do.
explanation: When ordering the Product Backlog, the Product Owner weighs alignment with business strategy, risk, dependencies with existing items, and importance to customers. The specific implementation techniques the Developers will use are their concern, not an ordering factor. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: At what point should a Product Backlog be refined?
options: Continuously, as needed.
During the Sprint Review only.
Once per month.
Before each release.
trap: Refinement is a continuous activity — not a per-release or monthly ceremony.
explanation: The best answer is continuously, as needed. Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity to keep items clear and ready - it is not confined to the Sprint Review, a monthly cadence, or a pre-release event. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: During Sprint Planning, a senior stakeholder insists on reordering the Product Backlog to prioritize their department's requests. The Developers agree it would be easier to build. Who has final accountability for the backlog ordering?
options: The stakeholder, because they understand business needs best
The Developers, because they know what is technically feasible
The Product Owner, who considers value, risk, and dependencies across all stakeholders
The Scrum Master, who facilitates the ordering process
trap: Neither seniority nor technical knowledge overrides the PO's ordering accountability.
explanation: The best answer is the Product Owner, who holds final accountability for Product Backlog ordering, weighing value, risk, and dependencies across all stakeholders. A single stakeholder's preference, the Developers' build convenience, or the Scrum Master's facilitation do not override that accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog) Question 131 Who defines a Definition of "Done"? Options & Réponses : ● ● ● ● [ ] The Product Owner. [ ] The organization's quality assurance group. [x] The Scrum Team. [ ] Scrum Master. Explication générale : The best answer is the Scrum Team. If the Definition of Done is an organizational standard, all teams follow it as a minimum; otherwise the Scrum Team creates one appropriate for the product. It is not defined solely by the Scrum Master, the Product Owner, or a separate QA group. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: What of these behaviors align with Scrum values?
options: Hiding performance problems.
Respecting different perspectives.
Encouraging open feedback.
Prioritizing personal goals over team goals.
trap: Hiding problems and personal agendas violate openness and commitment.
explanation: Encouraging open feedback and respecting different perspectives embody the Scrum values of openness and respect. Hiding performance problems or putting personal goals over team goals contradicts those values. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 4 - Scrum Values)

text: Which are signs that a Product Owner is not effectively maximizing value?
options: Stakeholders are confused about the direction.
Product Backlog lacks clear ordering.
Product Goals are clearly communicated.
Outcomes are improving with each Sprint.
trap: Clear goals and improving outcomes are healthy signs — confusion and unordered backlogs are the red flags.
explanation: An unclear or unordered Product Backlog and stakeholders confused about direction are signs the Product Owner is not effectively maximizing value. Improving outcomes each Sprint and clearly communicated Product Goals are signs of the opposite. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What would be the main reason for the Scrum Master to be at the Daily Scrum?
options: To gather status and progress information to report to management.
To write down any changes to the Sprint Backlog.
They do not have to be there; they only need to ensure the Developers have a Daily Scrum.
trap: The SM need not attend the Daily Scrum — it is the Developers' event; status collection is an anti-pattern.
explanation: The best answer is that the Scrum Master does not have to attend - they only need to ensure the Developers hold an effective Daily Scrum. The event is for the Developers; the Scrum Master attends as a Developer only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items, and never to gather status for management. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9 - Daily Scrum)

text: Which option below statements about a Product Backlog are true?
options: Only the Product Owner can place items on the Product Backlog.
The Product Backlog is ordered by the Product Owner.
The Product Backlog should be visible to the Scrum Team and stakeholders.
All Product Backlog items must be identified before the first Sprint begins.
The Product Backlog represents the input of all stakeholders and eliminates any need for the Developers to speak to stakeholders.
Every Product Backlog item must be expressed as user stories.
trap: Anyone can propose items and the backlog is never 'complete' — visibility and PO ordering are the truths.
explanation: The best answers are that the Product Backlog is ordered by the Product Owner and is visible to the Scrum Team and stakeholders. Items need not be user stories, need not all exist before the first Sprint, anyone can propose items, and the backlog never removes the need to talk with stakeholders. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: A Product Owner manages a product with four Scrum Teams and struggles to attend all events. Teams report feeling disconnected from the product direction. What is the best approach?
options: Appoint a separate Product Owner for each team to distribute the workload
Communicate a clear Product Goal and delegate specific backlog management activities to trusted Developers, while retaining accountability
Reduce the number of Scrum events to free up the Product Owner's schedule
Ask the Scrum Masters to take over Product Backlog ordering for their respective teams
trap: One PO per team and skipping Scrum events both break the framework — delegation solves the load.
explanation: The best answer is to communicate a clear Product Goal and delegate specific backlog activities to trusted Developers while retaining accountability. Appointing a Product Owner per team, cutting Scrum events, or handing ordering to Scrum Masters each fragment ownership or reduce transparency. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: The user satisfaction gap exists when there is a difference between which of the following?
options: The total market size.
The user's actual experience.
The user's desired outcome.
The market share of the product.
trap: The satisfaction gap is experience vs desired outcome — market size and share are different measures.
explanation: The best answer is that the user satisfaction gap is the difference between the user's desired outcome and their actual experience. Market share and total market size are not what defines that gap, though they may be affected by it. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Your competitor has lower market share but higher customer satisfaction and faster delivery. What should you do first in Scrum?
options: Lower your price.
Add more features.
Find new markets.
Improve your time-to-market and rate of innovation.
trap: Competing on price or feature count ignores what the competitor actually does better: speed and satisfaction.
explanation: The best answer is to improve your time-to-market and rate of innovation. When a competitor delivers faster with higher satisfaction, becoming more responsive lets you meet customer needs and adapt. Cutting price, chasing new markets, or piling on features does not address the underlying responsiveness gap. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Evaluate this statement: a Scrum Master is a management position.
options: False.
Correct.
trap: The Scrum Master leads by serving — it is not a management position.
explanation: The best answer is False. The Scrum Master is a true leader who serves the team and organization - a servant-leader accountable for the team's effectiveness and for establishing Scrum, not a manager of people or tasks. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 6-7 - Scrum Master)

text: You have usage data for a product, but a stakeholder doesn't trust it and wants to override the data. What step should you take?
options: Continue to measure and publish the data, to provide openness and transparency, and use it to inform your decisions.
Continue measuring feature usage and use it to inform your decisions, but do not publish it.
Stop measuring feature usage to appease the stakeholder.
trap: Suppressing or spinning data to appease a stakeholder destroys transparency — keep measuring and publishing.
explanation: The best answer is to continue measuring and publishing the data and use it to inform decisions. Transparency and empiricism are core to Scrum, so reliable data should be shared openly - not hidden to appease a stakeholder or measured privately without publishing. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Transparency)

text: The environment in which a product is used changes continually. What is the effect on the Product Backlog?
options: The Product Backlog evolves to reflect what the product needs to be most valuable.
There is no effect; the Product Backlog stays the same.
The Product Backlog is archived and a new Product Backlog is created.
The requirements document must be updated to ensure stability.
trap: The backlog is a living artifact — it evolves with the environment, it is never 'archived'.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Backlog evolves to reflect what the product needs to be most valuable. As the environment changes, the backlog adapts - it is not archived and replaced, left unchanged, or swapped for a static requirements document. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: A mature product has strong revenue but user growth has plateaued and no significant unmet needs remain in the market. What should the organization consider?
options: Doubling the investment to break through the plateau
Cancelling the product immediately since growth has stopped
Gradually reducing investment as the product's Unrealized Value is diminishing
Maintaining high investment because revenue is strong
trap: Plateaued growth with no unmet needs means low Unrealized Value — pouring more investment in chases nothing.
explanation: The best answer is to gradually reduce investment as the product's Unrealized Value diminishes. With a strong revenue base but no remaining unmet needs, further investment yields little, so resources are better freed for higher-opportunity products - not doubled down, maintained on revenue alone, or cut abruptly. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What would be the impact of technical debt on product value?
options: It guarantees better code reuse.
It increases delivery speed.
It may slow delivery and reduce future value.
It has no long-term effect.
trap: Technical debt silently erodes future value — 'no long-term effect' is the dangerous assumption.
explanation: The best answer is that technical debt may slow delivery and reduce future value. Deferred quality accumulates and hampers the team's ability to deliver reliably later - it does not increase speed, stay harmless, or guarantee reuse. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which are the accountabilities of a Tester on a Scrum Team?
options: Everyone on the Scrum Team is accountable for the quality of the product.
There is no specific tester role.
Checking the work of the Developers.
Finding bugs to assure quality.
Creating code coverage reports for the test manager.
trap: Quality is everyone's accountability — 'tester' is not a Scrum role.
explanation: The best answers are that there is no specific tester role and that everyone on the Scrum Team is accountable for quality. Scrum removes separate testing hand-offs such as coverage reports for a test manager, bug-finding as a distinct role, or checking the Developers' work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: Complete a sentence: The more uncertain you are about customer needs or market desires...
options: The smaller each release should be.
The more you should focus on validating customer needs.
The more likely it is that you should invest in a different product.
The more important a risk management plan becomes.
trap: More uncertainty calls for smaller releases and validation — not bigger plans or more risk paperwork.
explanation: The best answers are that greater uncertainty means you should focus more on validating customer needs and make each release smaller. Smaller, faster releases and experimentation validate assumptions and limit risk - uncertainty is not a reason to abandon the product or add a heavy risk-management plan. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: Which metric would be most useful for measuring Time-to-Market?
options: Number of team members.
Number of Sprints per release.
Lead time from idea to delivery.
Burn-down chart.
trap: Time-to-Market is lead time from idea to delivery — Sprint counts and burndowns don't measure it.
explanation: The best answer is lead time from idea to delivery, which is exactly what Time-to-Market measures. The number of Sprints per release, team size, or a burndown chart do not capture how long value takes to reach customers. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What techniques can the Product Owner use to identify valuable features?
options: Stakeholder interviews.
Competitor analysis.
Developer intuition.
Usage analytics.
trap: Developer intuition alone doesn't identify value — triangulate with users, competitors and data.
explanation: Identifying valuable features draws on stakeholder interviews, usage analytics, and competitor analysis - multiple sources of evidence. Relying on developer intuition alone is risky and not evidence-based. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 Product Owner)

text: A Scrum Team's Sprint burndown chart shows remaining work increasing at mid-Sprint. The Scrum Master raises this at the Daily Scrum. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: The team has discovered additional complexity or refined their understanding of the remaining work
The burndown chart is unreliable and should be replaced
The Developers are underperforming and need closer management
The Sprint Goal should be changed to match the new reality
trap: Rising burndown usually means discovered complexity — jumping to 'underperformance' or changing the Goal are traps.
explanation: The best answer is that the Developers have discovered additional complexity or refined their understanding of the remaining work. A burndown makes remaining work transparent so the team can inspect and adapt; a mid-Sprint rise is not proof of underperformance, an unreliable chart, or a reason to change the Sprint Goal. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9 - Daily Scrum)

text: At what point is it most appropriate for a Development Team to change the Definition of "Done"?
options: During the Daily Scrum.
Prior to starting a new Sprint.
During the Sprint Retrospective.
Prior to starting a new project.
trap: The DoD is inspected and adapted at the Retrospective — not mid-execution at the Daily Scrum.
explanation: The best answer is during the Sprint Retrospective, where the Scrum Team inspects its way of working - including the Definition of Done - and agrees on improvements. Changing it in the Daily Scrum, arbitrarily before a Sprint, or before a 'project' would bypass that shared, deliberate inspection. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: What would be the impact of a missing Sprint Goal?
options: Developers lack focus and shared direction.
Nothing - the Sprint proceeds normally.
The Product Owner loses authority.
The Sprint is shorter.
trap: Without a Sprint Goal the Sprint loses focus and coherence — it does not proceed 'normally'.
explanation: The best answer is that the Developers lack focus and shared direction. The Sprint Goal creates coherence and focus; without it, Developers may work on unrelated tasks. It does not shorten the Sprint, strip the Product Owner's authority, or leave the Sprint unaffected. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: Determine if this is accurate: A Product Owner should be familiar with a definition of "Done."
options: False.
Correct.
trap: The PO must know the DoD — release decisions depend on understanding what 'Done' guarantees.
explanation: The best answer is Correct. The Product Owner must understand the Definition of Done to manage the Product Backlog well and make informed decisions about what can be accomplished, since the Definition of Done creates the transparency the Product Owner relies on to maximize value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: In what way does a Product Owner support Developers during a Sprint?
options: By setting work hours.
By validating code.
By assigning tasks daily.
By staying available to clarify backlog items.
trap: The PO supports by being available for clarification — not by policing hours or code.
explanation: The best answer is by staying available to clarify Product Backlog items. The Product Owner supports value delivery through clarity, not by assigning tasks daily, validating code, or setting the Developers' work hours. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What enhances the transparency of an Increment?
options: Keeping track of and estimating all undone work to be completed in a "hardening" Sprint.
Updating Sprint tasks properly in the electronic tracking tool.
Doing all work needed to meet the Definition of "Done.".
Reporting Sprint progress to stakeholders daily.
trap: Transparency of the Increment comes from truly meeting the DoD — not from tracking undone work or reporting.
explanation: The best answer is doing all the work needed to meet the Definition of Done, which makes the Increment's true state transparent. Tracking undone work for a 'hardening' Sprint, daily status reports, or diligent tool updates do not create the same transparency about what is genuinely complete. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)

text: Which are characteristics of an effective Sprint Goal?
options: Changes daily based on team preference.
Guides the work during the Sprint.
Specific and focused.
Negotiated with stakeholders mid-Sprint.
trap: A Sprint Goal negotiated or rewritten mid-Sprint stops being a stable commitment.
explanation: An effective Sprint Goal is specific and focused and guides the work throughout the Sprint. It is not renegotiated with stakeholders mid-Sprint or changed daily on team preference - its stability is what creates coherence. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: How often should a Scrum Team inspect and adapt?
options: Only when management requests.
At least once per Sprint.
Once per release.
Every six weeks.
trap: Inspection/adaptation happens at least every Sprint — waiting for releases or management is too slow.
explanation: The best answer is at least once per Sprint. Scrum builds inspection and adaptation into every Sprint through the Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective - not once per release, on a fixed six-week cycle, or only on management request. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 4 - Inspection)

text: Which option best describes a Product Owner's responsibility?
options: Optimizing the value of the work the Scrum Team does.
Directing the Developers.
Keeping stakeholders at bay.
Managing the project and ensuring work meets the commitments to stakeholders.
trap: The PO optimizes value — directing Developers or fencing off stakeholders is not the accountability.
explanation: The best answer is optimizing the value of the work the Scrum Team does. The Product Owner maximizes product value rather than directing the Developers, managing the project to stakeholder commitments, or keeping stakeholders at arm's length. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What actions reduce Product Backlog clutter?
options: Deleting old items without discussion.
Regular refinement sessions.
Avoiding stakeholder input.
Prioritizing based on strategic goals.
trap: Deleting items without discussion or excluding stakeholders reduces clutter at the cost of trust and value.
explanation: Regular refinement and prioritizing by strategic goals reduce Product Backlog clutter while preserving value. Deleting items without discussion or avoiding stakeholder input removes information the team needs to order the backlog well. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: Currently, your Development Teams are organized to address the single functional layer only. What are three things to consider when deciding to move away from such component teams toward feature teams?
options: With feature teams, the Development Teams work more closely with the business.
Productivity may decrease when making the shift.
Feature teams have less communication overhead.
Getting support from the business side first helps.
You cannot do Scrum without feature teams.
trap: Feature teams trade short-term productivity dips for customer proximity — expecting less overhead immediately is the trap.
explanation: The best answer is that with feature teams the Developers work more closely with the business. Feature teams are cross-functional and deliver complete features end-to-end, reducing hand-offs. Scrum does not strictly require feature teams, and while transitions can temporarily dip productivity, the closer business collaboration is the key consideration. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: A Product Owner has 40 items in the Product Backlog. Stakeholders from marketing, engineering, and compliance each argue their items should be top priority. What is the Product Owner's most important backlog management activity in this situation?
options: Freeze the backlog until all stakeholders reach consensus
Give each stakeholder group equal representation in the top 10 items
Order items based on evidence of value, risk, and alignment with the Product Goal
Let the Developers choose the order based on technical complexity
trap: Freezing the backlog or seeking consensus paralysis — the PO orders by evidence, not by committee.
explanation: The best answer is to order items based on evidence of value, risk, and alignment with the Product Goal. That is the Product Owner's core backlog-management activity when stakeholders compete for priority. Equal representation, delegating ordering to Developers, or freezing the backlog for consensus all undermine accountability and delay value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What tools support inspection in Scrum ?
options: Burn-down charts.
Daily Scrum.
Sprint Review.
Gantt charts.
trap: Gantt charts plan; they don't support empirical inspection.
explanation: Sprint Review, burn-down charts, and the Daily Scrum all support inspection by making progress visible. Gantt charts are predictive planning tools and do not provide the empirical inspection Scrum relies on. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 4 Inspection)

text: What could signal poor backlog management?
options: Items are continuously refined.
Backlog items lack clear acceptance criteria.
Items are not ordered by value.
Items are updated based on new information.
trap: Continuous refinement and updates are good signs — the flags are missing criteria and value-blind ordering.
explanation: Backlog items lacking clear acceptance criteria and items not ordered by value are signs of poor backlog management, because they reduce transparency and misdirect effort. Continuous refinement and updating items on new information are healthy practices, not warning signs. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: You validated multiple stakeholder feature requests. How would you best proceed in Scrum?
options: Wait until all essential features are complete before releasing the product.
Escalate to the steering committee.
Deploy when you can satisfy at least a single outcome, even though not all features are implemented.
Pick the two most influential stakeholders and satisfy their needs.
trap: Waiting for 'all essential features' postpones all value — a single satisfied outcome justifies deployment.
explanation: The best answer is to deploy once you can satisfy at least one valuable outcome, even if not all features are implemented. Scrum favors early, incremental delivery to gather feedback and reduce risk - rather than pleasing the most influential stakeholders, waiting for everything, or escalating. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: At what point does the next Sprint begin?
options: Next Monday.
Immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
When the Product Owner is ready.
Immediately following the next Sprint Planning.
trap: There is no pause: the next Sprint begins immediately, not after a planning gap or a PO green light.
explanation: The best answer is immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint. There is no gap between Sprints, which keeps momentum and regular inspection - it does not wait for Monday, the Product Owner's readiness, or the next Sprint Planning. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: What would be the main purpose of the Product Backlog?
options: To describe all the tasks Developers must complete.
To list team assignments.
To keep technical documentation.
To provide transparency about future product work.
trap: The Product Backlog creates transparency on future work — it is not a task list or documentation store.
explanation: The best answer is to provide transparency about future product work. The Product Backlog is a transparent, evolving list of what will improve the product not a place for technical documentation, an exhaustive task list, or team assignments. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: To increase a likelihood of improving the retention rate, what additional measurements should you consider when determining improvements?
options: All of the above.
The On-Product Index, the ratio of product work to total work.
Employee Net Promoter Scores.
The Innovation Rate, which is the ratio of new work to total work.
trap: Retention improvement needs multiple Ability-to-Innovate measures together — no single metric suffices.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Innovation Rate, the On-Product Index, and employee Net Promoter Score together show whether Developers are doing meaningful, valuable work and feel engaged - the drivers behind retention. No single metric captures all three. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What would be the recommended size for a Scrum Team?
options: At least seven.
7 plus or minus 2.
10 or fewer.
trap: The Scrum Guide says 10 or fewer — '7±2' is folklore, not the Guide.
explanation: The best answer is 10 or fewer people. A Scrum Team is small enough to stay nimble yet large enough to do significant work in a Sprint - roughly ten or fewer, including the Product Owner, Scrum Master, and Developers. Fixed formulas like 'seven plus or minus two' are not the Scrum Guide's guidance. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: Developer retention would be dropping, and exit interviews reveal frustration with low-value work. What measurements could help?
options: On-Product Index.
Employee Net Promoter Scores.
All of the above.
Innovation Rate.
trap: Low-value work frustration is measured through several EBM lenses combined, not one favorite metric.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Innovation Rate, the On-Product Index, and employee Net Promoter Score each illuminate a different facet of engagement and meaningful work, so considering them together gives the fullest picture of what is affecting retention. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide Key Value Areas)

text: Who builds the Increment?
options: The Scrum Team.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
trap: The Developers build the Increment — the whole Scrum Team is accountable, but the building is theirs.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers, who are the people committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint. The whole Scrum Team is accountable for the Increment, but the Developers are the ones who build it - not the Scrum Master or Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Developers)

text: An organization has three Scrum Teams building a single payment platform. Each team currently maintains its own backlog. Customer features frequently require coordination across teams, causing delays. What change would most improve this situation?
options: Let each team deliver independently and integrate quarterly
Consolidate into one shared Product Backlog with one Product Owner to ensure consistent ordering and alignment
Merge all teams into one large Scrum Team for better coordination
Add a project manager to coordinate across the three backlogs
trap: Multiple backlogs for one product fragment value — one product, one Product Backlog, one PO.
explanation: The best answer is to consolidate into one shared Product Backlog with one Product Owner to ensure consistent ordering and alignment. Multiple teams on the same product share one backlog and one Product Owner. Merging teams violates the size guidance, a project manager is not a Scrum role, and quarterly integration delays feedback. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: Which are common anti-patterns for Product Ownership?
options: Frequently inspecting outcomes.
Being unavailable to the team.
Working closely with stakeholders.
Delegating backlog prioritization to Developers.
trap: Working with stakeholders and inspecting outcomes are healthy — absence and abdicating ordering are the anti-patterns.
explanation: Delegating backlog prioritization to the Developers and being unavailable to the team are common Product Owner anti-patterns, because they abdicate the ordering accountability and cut off collaboration. Working closely with stakeholders and inspecting outcomes are good practices, not anti-patterns. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Which person's role includes for tracking the remaining work for the Increment in the Sprint?
options: The Scrum Team.
The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.
The Project Manager.
The Developers.
trap: Tracking remaining Sprint work belongs to the Developers — not the SM, PO or a project manager.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers. They self-manage their work and track remaining work toward the Sprint Goal in the Sprint Backlog. This is not the Scrum Master's, a project manager's, the Product Owner's, or the whole team's task. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Backlog)

text: What is the main responsibility of a Product Owner?
options: Writing User Stories that the Scrum Team can fully understand.
Maximizing the value of the work that the Scrum Team delivers.
Managing the Product Backlog.
Interfacing between the Developers and the customers.
trap: Managing the backlog and writing stories are activities — the accountability is maximizing value.
explanation: The best answer is maximizing the value of the work the Scrum Team delivers. Managing the Product Backlog serves that higher goal; writing user stories or acting as a go-between are secondary to the value accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What describes the minimum Product Increment that is valuable enough to release?
options: Delivers all "must do" Product Backlog items.
Fixes at least one defect.
Adds a new feature.
Provides a single new or improved outcome.
trap: A minimum valuable release delivers one improved outcome — not 'all must-do items' or any arbitrary feature.
explanation: The best answer is that a releasable Increment provides a single new or improved outcome. An Increment must be usable and valuable, and even one meaningful outcome can be worth releasing - it does not require fixing a defect, adding a feature, or delivering every 'must-do' item. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: Which behaviors help the Product Owner lead in a complex environment?
options: Making evidence-based decisions.
Avoiding technical discussions.
Collaborating closely with stakeholders.
Commanding the team to meet deadlines.
trap: Command-and-control and avoiding technical conversations both weaken PO leadership in complexity.
explanation: Leading in complexity means collaborating closely with stakeholders and making evidence-based decisions. Commanding the team to hit deadlines or avoiding technical discussions works against empiricism and self-management. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: For what reason is it important that there is only one Product Owner per product? (select three correct answers)
options: It helps avoid barriers to effective communication and rapid decision-making.
It helps the economy by increasing employment.
The Developers always know who determines the order of the Product Backlog.
It is obvious who is accountable for the ultimate success of the product.
The Scrum Master knows who acts as their backup while on vacation.
trap: Extra POs don't create jobs or backups — one PO exists for clear accountability and fast decisions.
explanation: One Product Owner per product makes accountability clear, avoids communication barriers so decisions are made quickly, and lets the Developers always know who orders the Product Backlog. Providing a vacation backup or boosting employment are not reasons Scrum gives for a single Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What would Unrealized Value represent in Evidence-Based Management?
options: The cost of development.
Profit from current customers.
The potential value that could be realized in the future.
The team's burn rate.
trap: Unrealized Value is future potential — not current profit, cost or burn rate.
explanation: The best answer is the potential value that could be realized in the future. Unrealized Value represents the upside still available if the market's or users' needs were more fully met - not current profit, development cost, or burn rate. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Who owns a Sprint Backlog?
options: Scrum Master.
The Developers.
The Scrum Team.
The Product Owner.
trap: The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers alone — not the whole Scrum Team.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers. The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers, so they own it and manage it throughout the Sprint. It is not owned by the Scrum Master, the Product Owner, or the Scrum Team as a whole. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Backlog)

text: At what point is a Product Backlog item considered complete?
options: When the item has no work remaining in order to be released.
When the Definition of "Done" is applied and the item is usable.
When QA reports that the item meets their quality criteria.
At the end of the Sprint.
trap: QA sign-off or Sprint end don't complete an item — only the DoD does.
explanation: The best answer is when the Definition of Done is applied and the item is usable. The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born - completeness is not defined by 'no work left to release', the Sprint's end, or a QA sign-off alone. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done) Voici l'extraction au format texte avec la suite continue de la numérotation (de 181 à 190) :

text: A distinct Product Backlog is needed for every what?
options: Program.
A product.
Portfolio.
All of the above.
Scrum Team.
trap: Backlogs map to products — not to programs, portfolios or teams.
explanation: The best answer is a product. Each product has one Product Backlog; multiple Scrum Teams working on the same product share it, rather than having a separate backlog per team, portfolio, or program. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 Product Backlog)

text: When should the Product Owner cancel a Sprint?
options: There is a change in the CEO.
The stakeholders ask for a new Sprint to start immediately.
The Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
The Scrum Master determines there are impediments that cannot be removed.
The Developers cannot complete the Sprint Backlog.
trap: CEO changes, stakeholder requests or impediments don't cancel Sprints — only an obsolete Sprint Goal does.
explanation: The best answer is when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete - and only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint. A change in leadership, an incomplete Sprint Backlog, unremovable impediments, or a stakeholder request are not reasons to cancel. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: For the purpose of transparency, when does Scrum say a new Increment must be available?
options: Before the release Sprint.
After the acceptance testing phase.
At the end of every Sprint.
When Product Owner requests to create one.
Every 3 Sprints.
trap: A new Increment exists at latest by Sprint end — not after test phases or on request.
explanation: The best answer is at the end of every Sprint. A usable Increment must be available each Sprint to support inspection and adaptation at the Sprint Review not only when the Product Owner asks, before a release Sprint, or on a multi-Sprint cadence. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: Determine if this is accurate: The Product Owner is a Scrum Team member who must be present at the Sprint Retrospective.
options: False.
Correct.
trap: The PO is a Scrum Team member but is NOT required at the Daily Scrum.
explanation: The best answer is False. The Sprint Retrospective is for the whole Scrum Team, so the Product Owner is expected to take part - but the Scrum Guide does not single out any one individual as one who 'must' be present; the focus is on the team's collective participation. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10 - Sprint Retrospective)

text: A Development Team informs the Product Owner during the Sprint that they are not likely to complete everything they forecasted. What should typically occur a Product Owner to do?
options: Change the Sprint Goal.
Skip Product Backlog polishing activities.
Inform management that more resources are needed.
Cancel the Sprint.
Re-negotiate the selected Product Backlog items with the Development Team to meet the Sprint Goal.
trap: Changing the Sprint Goal or calling for resources mid-Sprint breaks the frame — scope is renegotiated within it.
explanation: The best answer is to re-negotiate the selected Product Backlog items with the Developers to still meet the Sprint Goal. Scope may be clarified and renegotiated within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal - the team does not skip refinement, demand resources, change the Goal, or cancel the Sprint. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: A SaaS product shows strong sign-up numbers but 70% of users churn within 30 days. The Developers suggest building more features to increase retention. What should the Product Owner do first?
options: Ask stakeholders which features they believe will reduce churn
Approve building more features because a larger feature set typically improves retention
Increase the Sprint length to allow more thorough feature development
Investigate whether the current product delivers on the promise that attracted users in the first place
trap: Strong sign-ups with high churn is a value problem — building more features answers the wrong question.
explanation: The best answer is to first investigate whether the current product delivers on the promise that attracted users. Empiricism requires inspecting outcomes before adapting the plan; high sign-ups with high churn point to a Current Value gap. Adding features, lengthening the Sprint, or polling stakeholders skips the needed investigation. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: Halfway through a Sprint, the Developers realize they cannot complete all selected items. They ask the Product Owner: 'What should we prioritize?' What guides this conversation?
options: The Sprint Goal — it provides the overarching objective that helps decide which items to keep and which to negotiate
The Scrum Master's assessment of team capacity
The stakeholder who made the original request for each item
The burndown chart projection
trap: When everything can't be done, the Sprint Goal arbitrates — not the burndown, the SM or a stakeholder.
explanation: The best answer is the Sprint Goal. When scope must be reduced, the Sprint Goal is the reference for deciding which items are essential to the objective and which can be renegotiated. The burndown, the Scrum Master's capacity view, and the original requesters are not the guiding reference. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: What could signal to a Product Owner that they need to work more with the Scrum Team?
options: People frequently leave the Scrum Team.
They are not working full time with the Scrum Team.
The Increment presented at the Sprint Review does not reflect their expectations.
The acceptance criteria for the Product Backlog items do not appear to be complete.
trap: The clearest signal is an Increment that misses expectations — turnover or part-time presence are weaker signals.
explanation: The best answer is that the Increment presented at the Sprint Review does not reflect the Product Owner's expectations.
