That mismatch signals a need for closer collaboration during refinement and development. Part-time presence, incomplete acceptance criteria, or turnover are weaker signals of this specific gap. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review)

text: In what ways can personas help?
options: Understand market potential.
All of the above.
Discover key buying triggers.
Understand the needs of a set of users.
Formulate hypotheses about product value.
trap: Personas serve multiple purposes at once — picking a single use undersells them.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Personas help teams understand user needs, gauge market potential, discover buying triggers, and form hypotheses about value. They are a complementary practice that supports empirical product development, though the Scrum Guide does not prescribe them. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What is the proper way for a Product Owner to respond to significant negative customer feedback?
options: Investigate feedback patterns and adjust the Product Backlog.
Remove the Product Goal immediately.
Refer to management and wait for direction.
Ignore it until the next Sprint Review.
trap: Negative feedback is data — waiting for management or the next Review wastes the learning.
explanation: The best answer is to investigate the feedback patterns and adjust the Product Backlog. The Product Owner inspects feedback and adapts empirically rather than waiting for management, dropping the Product Goal, or ignoring input until the next Review. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: What of these support evidence-based management?
options: Unrealized Value.
Time-to-Market.
Current Value.
Velocity charts.
trap: Velocity charts measure team throughput — they are not EBM evidence of value.
explanation: Current Value, Unrealized Value, and Time-to-Market are Evidence-Based Management measures that support value-based decisions. A velocity chart is a local team metric, not an EBM Key Value Area. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Which are valid commitments in Scrum?
options: Release Plan.
Product Goal.
Sprint Goal.
Definition of Done.
trap: The Release Plan is not a Scrum commitment — Product Goal, Sprint Goal and DoD are.
explanation: The three Scrum commitments are the Sprint Goal (for the Sprint Backlog), the Definition of Done (for the Increment), and the Product Goal (for the Product Backlog). A release plan is not a Scrum commitment. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-12 - Scrum Artifacts / Commitments)

text: In what way can a Product Owner reduce waste in the product development process?
options: Focus on outcomes over output.
Validate assumptions before building.
Minimize stakeholder collaboration.
Maximize work-in-progress.
trap: Maximizing WIP and minimizing collaboration create waste — the opposite of lean product thinking.
explanation: Validating assumptions before building and focusing on outcomes over output reduce waste by preventing low-value work. Maximizing work-in-progress and minimizing stakeholder collaboration create waste and cut off the feedback that guides value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: Why should a Product Owner be available during the Sprint?
options: To ensure tasks are completed.
To track productivity.
To clarify Product Backlog items.
To assign work to Developers.
trap: The PO is available to clarify — not to supervise, track or assign.
explanation: The best answer is to clarify Product Backlog items. During the Sprint the Product Owner keeps the team aligned to value by answering questions and clarifying priorities - not by assigning work, ensuring task completion, or tracking productivity. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: An investor asks the Product Owner: 'How do I know your product is worth continued investment?' Which combination of measures best answers this question?
options: Revenue per employee, market share, competitive pricing position, and product profitability
Number of Product Backlog items refined and Sprint Goals achieved
Sprint velocity and number of Scrum events held per month
Lines of code deployed and number of releases per quarter
trap: Backlog counts, velocity and lines of code impress no investor — business outcomes do.
explanation: The best answer is revenue per employee, market share, competitive pricing position, and product profitability - business outcomes that show whether the product creates sustainable value. Velocity, event counts, items refined, or lines of code and release counts are activity or output measures, not value evidence. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What can happen if there's no clear Product Goal in Scrum?
options: The team can't work at all.
Sprint Planning becomes disjointed.
Team lacks long-term direction.
Releases still provide value regardless.
trap: Teams still function without a Product Goal — the cost is direction and coherent planning, not total paralysis.
explanation: Without a clear Product Goal the team loses long-term direction and Sprint Planning becomes disjointed, because there is no shared objective to plan against. Work can still happen, so it is an overstatement to say releases are automatically valuable or that the team cannot work at all. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: In what way is success measured in an agile product context?
options: Finishing all features on time.
Delivering value and outcomes to users.
Meeting project deadlines.
Reducing developer hours.
trap: Deadlines met and features shipped are output — agile success is user value and outcomes.
explanation: The best answer is delivering value and outcomes to users. Agile success is measured by outcomes, not by finishing all features on time, meeting deadlines, or reducing developer hours. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner) Voici l'extraction au format texte avec la suite continue de la numérotation (de 201 à 210) :

text: A Product Owner has three product ideas, each targeting a different market segment. Budget allows fully funding only one. Market data is limited. What approach best reduces investment risk?
options: Run small, time-boxed experiments for each idea to gather real market evidence before committing the full budget
Split the budget equally across all three ideas regardless of market signals
Choose the idea with the most executive support and fully fund it
Delay all investment until comprehensive market research is completed
trap: Executive support and equal budget splits are politics — small experiments produce evidence.
explanation: The best answer is to run small, time-boxed experiments for each idea to gather real market evidence before committing the full budget. This lean approach reduces waste by learning before scaling - unlike delaying for exhaustive research, funding by executive support, or splitting the budget evenly regardless of signals. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: A stakeholder references last Sprint's forecast during a review and asks why two items were not delivered. The Developers explain they discovered unexpected complexity. What is the correct interpretation of a Sprint forecast?
options: The forecast was a commitment; the team should have delivered everything
The forecast is a prediction based on current knowledge and may change as the team learns more during the Sprint
The Scrum Master failed to protect the team from scope changes
The forecast should be padded with buffer items to avoid this situation
trap: A forecast is not a commitment — treating misses as broken promises poisons empiricism.
explanation: The best answer is that the forecast is a prediction based on current understanding, not a commitment. If the work turns out differently, scope is renegotiated with the Product Owner. Padding with buffers or blaming the Scrum Master misreads what a forecast is. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning)

text: A Product Owner must decide whether to release an Increment that contains only a single improved workflow. A stakeholder argues it is too small to release. What should guide the decision?
options: The Increment should be released if it provides a meaningful outcome for users, regardless of size
The Increment should only be released when it contains at least five new features
The Increment must wait until the next Sprint for additional features to be added
The Scrum Master decides when an Increment is large enough to release
trap: Value density beats size — a single meaningful improvement justifies release; waiting or delegating the call does not.
explanation: The best answer is to release the Increment if it provides a meaningful outcome for users, regardless of size. Even a single improved workflow can be worth releasing - size thresholds, a Scrum Master gatekeeper, or automatic deferral to the next Sprint are not how release value is judged. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11-12 - Increment)

text: When is the appropriate time for a Sprint Goal to be created?
options: It should have been created in the previous Sprint during Product Backlog refinement.
It must be established before Sprint Planning to give guidance to the Development Team on what to build.
During Sprint Planning.
At any time during the Sprint.
trap: The Sprint Goal is created during Sprint Planning — never before, never later.
explanation: The best answer is during Sprint Planning. The Sprint Goal is created by the whole Scrum Team during Sprint Planning and must be finalized before the event ends - not in the previous Sprint, at any arbitrary time, or before planning begins. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: Which behaviors help Developers and Product Owner collaborate effectively in Scrum?
options: Product Owner assigning tasks daily.
Open discussions during refinement.
Shared understanding of priorities.
Avoiding conflicts and feedback.
trap: A PO who assigns tasks daily or a team that avoids feedback both corrode collaboration.
explanation: A shared understanding of priorities and open discussions during refinement help the Product Owner and Developers collaborate. Avoiding conflict and feedback, or having the Product Owner assign daily tasks, undermine transparency and self-management. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: You are coaching the new Product Owner. Which advice is most helpful?
options: Focus on optimizing the work of the Developers.
Defer decision-making to the Scrum Master when under pressure.
Create a separate backlog for each stakeholder group.
Align the Product Backlog to measurable outcomes and business goals.
trap: Advising a new PO to optimize Developer work or defer to the SM misdirects the accountability.
explanation: The best answer is to align the Product Backlog to measurable outcomes and business goals. Effective Product Ownership focuses on value, not on optimizing the Developers' work, splitting the backlog per stakeholder group, or deferring decisions to the Scrum Master under pressure. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What factors might influence the ordering of Product Backlog items?
options: Developer preference.
Technical risk.
Customer feedback.
Strategic goals.
trap: Developer preference doesn't order the backlog — risk, feedback and strategy do.
explanation: Customer feedback, technical risk, and strategic goals all legitimately influence how the Product Owner orders the Product Backlog. Developer preference is not an ordering factor - ordering is driven by value, risk, and alignment, not personal preference. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: A new Product Goal has been defined. What should happen next in Scrum?
options: The team must create a new Product Backlog from scratch.
Developers must reorganize into new teams.
The Sprint Goal should automatically change.
The Product Backlog should evolve to reflect the new direction.
trap: A new Product Goal evolves the existing backlog — it doesn't spawn a new backlog or reshuffle teams.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Backlog should evolve to reflect the new direction. A new Product Goal guides the backlog, which adapts accordingly the team does not rebuild the backlog from scratch, automatically change the Sprint Goal, or reorganize into new teams. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: What is the timebox for the Sprint Review?
options: At the end of every Sprint.
Any length of time needed.
15 minutes.
4 hours for a 4-week Sprint. Usually shorter for shorter Sprints.
trap: Four hours max for a month-long Sprint — 15 minutes is the Daily Scrum, not the Review.
explanation: The best answer is a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint, and usually shorter for shorter Sprints. The Sprint Review is timeboxed, not open-ended; '15 minutes' is the Daily Scrum, and 'at the end of every Sprint' describes when it occurs, not its length. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review) Voici l'extraction au format texte avec la suite continue de la numérotation (de 211 à 220) :

options: Ensure that all 3 questions have been answered.
Facilitate in a way that ensures each team member has a chance to speak.
Lead the discussions of the Developers.
All of the above.
Teach the Developers to keep the Daily Scrum within the 15-minute timebox.

explanation: The best answer is to teach the Developers to keep the Daily Scrum within its 15-minute timebox. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 6-7 - Scrum Master)

text: A Product Owner wants to convince the board that the latest release improved customer value. Which evidence would be most compelling?
options: Reduction in customer support tickets and increase in feature adoption rates
The team's average velocity over the last four Sprints
Total number of Product Backlog items marked as Done
Number of story points completed during the release Sprint
trap: Velocity and story points won't convince a board — customer-facing evidence will.
explanation: The best answer is the reduction in customer support tickets and the increase in feature adoption - outcome metrics that reflect real customer value. Story points completed, average velocity, and items marked Done are output measures that do not demonstrate value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide Key Value Areas)

text: A Product Owner has built detailed personas and uses them to justify every backlog decision without seeking additional customer input. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Stakeholders gain more influence because personas formalize their input
The Scrum Team delivers faster because fewer feedback loops are needed
Product decisions gradually drift from real user needs because assumptions go unvalidated
The Product Backlog becomes well-ordered because personas provide stable priorities
trap: Personas built once become fiction over time — without refreshed research, decisions drift from real users.
explanation: The best answer is that product decisions gradually drift from real users when personas are used to justify every choice without ongoing validation. Personas are an aid, not a substitute for empirical feedback - so they do not automatically produce a well-ordered backlog, grant stakeholders influence, or make delivery faster. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What would be the Product Owner accountable for?
options: Ensuring the work meets quality standards.
Managing the team's performance.
Defining technical solutions.
Maximizing the value of the product.
trap: Quality standards, team performance and technical choices belong to others — the PO owns value.
explanation: According to the Scrum Guide, the Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product. Managing team performance, ensuring quality standards, and defining technical solutions are not the Product Owner's accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: A Product Owner is launching a B2B product with three distinct buyer segments. Early feedback is contradictory. How should personas be used in this situation?
options: Create personas and use them as the primary source of product decisions
Use personas to identify patterns across segments and guide Product Backlog ordering, while continuing to validate with real feedback
Skip personas and rely solely on quantitative usage data
Build personas to document stakeholder opinions so they feel heard
trap: Personas guide but never replace validation with real users — treating them as the sole source is the trap.
explanation: The best answer is to use personas to identify patterns across segments while grounding decisions in real customer feedback. Personas complement - not replace - empirical validation, so treating them as the primary source, skipping them entirely, or using them merely to document opinions all miss the point. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What of these options are required by Scrum?
options: Project Gantt chart.
Burndown chart.
Critical Path Analysis.
Feature burn-up.
Refactoring.
None of the above.
trap: Scrum mandates none of these tools — charts and refactoring are complementary practices, not requirements.
explanation: The best answer is none of the above. Scrum prescribes no specific tools or techniques such as burndown charts, critical-path analysis, refactoring, Gantt charts, or feature burn-ups - teams choose methods that support transparency and empiricism. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 7-8 - The Sprint)

text: You are the new Product Owner. Many people expect to be involved in your decisions. What are reasonable steps you could take?
options: Let others make decisions and document when they fail.
Share a delegation board to clarify accountability.
Work with your Scrum Master to move product ownership maturity forward.
Demonstrate, with data, how delays in decision-making affect delivery.
Start making all decisions without consulting anyone.
trap: Letting others decide 'to prove a point' or going it alone both fail — structure delegation and show the cost of delay.
explanation: Reasonable steps for a new Product Owner are to demonstrate with data how slow decisions hurt delivery, share a delegation board to clarify accountability, and work with the Scrum Master to advance product-ownership maturity. Making all decisions in isolation or documenting others' failures neither builds trust nor improves decision-making. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What would be the most effective way to manage stakeholder expectations?
options: Avoid surprises by making no changes.
Rely solely on contracts.
Share progress frequently and invite feedback.
Stick to the initial scope no matter what.
trap: Contracts and frozen scope don't manage expectations — frequent transparency does.
explanation: The best answer is to share progress frequently and invite feedback. Frequent inspection keeps stakeholders aligned as goals evolve and builds trust. Making no changes, relying solely on contracts, or rigidly sticking to the original scope all reduce transparency and collaboration. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Transparency)

text: Who would be accountable for engaging the stakeholders to ensure value is delivered?
options: The business analyst since they are the Subject Matter Expert.
The project manager schedules all stakeholder interactions.
The Product Owner is responsible, but engagement can be delegated.
The team manager is responsible for managing the time spent with stakeholders.
The Developers are responsible for all stakeholder engagement.
trap: Stakeholder engagement can be delegated but the accountability stays with the PO — never with a BA or PM.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Owner is accountable for engaging stakeholders, but the engagement itself can be delegated. Accountability cannot be transferred, only the activity. It is not a business analyst's, team manager's, project manager's, or the Developers' accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: Which three statements accurately describe a relationship between the Product Owner and Developers during Sprint Planning?
options: The Product Owner decides exactly how the Developers will implement each item.
The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value in the current Sprint.
The Developers select Product Backlog items to include in the Sprint after discussion with the Product Owner.
The whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner must approve each Developer's individual work plan.
The Product Owner assigns specific tasks to individual Developers.
trap: The PO proposes value and the Developers select and self-manage — approval and task assignment are fiction.
explanation: During Sprint Planning the Product Owner proposes how the product could increase value, the Developers select the Product Backlog items for the Sprint, and the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal. The Product Owner does not assign individual tasks, dictate how the work is done, or approve each Developer's work. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning)

text: In what way can the Product Owner reduce delivery risk?
options: By delaying release decisions.
By releasing less frequently.
By validating assumptions early.
By involving stakeholders in Reviews.
trap: Delaying decisions and releasing less often increase risk — the reverse of risk reduction.
explanation: Validating assumptions early and involving stakeholders in Sprint Reviews reduce the risk of building the wrong thing, because feedback arrives sooner. Releasing less frequently or delaying release decisions lengthens feedback loops and increases risk. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9-10 - Sprint Review)

text: What sources of information should you consider when deciding whether to drop the price as the Sales Leader is suggesting? (select four accurate answers)
options: Competitor pricing.
Unmet customer needs.
Channel sales strategy.
Client satisfaction.
Market share.
Company earnings targets.
trap: Internal targets (earnings, channel strategy) don't inform a pricing response — market evidence does.
explanation: A value-based pricing decision draws on client satisfaction, market share, unmet customer needs, and competitor pricing - evidence about customers and the market. Internal earnings targets and the channel sales strategy alone are not sufficient grounds for a value-based decision. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: From the following options, which are characteristics of a Product Goal?
options: It has the approval of all stakeholders.
It forms a contract with the business, allowing change to be better managed.
It communicates the target future state of the product.
It is a commitment contained in the Product Backlog.
It enhances focus.
It provides a long-term objective for the Scrum Team to plan against.
trap: The Product Goal needs no universal stakeholder approval and is not a contract.
explanation: The Product Goal communicates the target future state of the product, enhances focus, is the commitment contained in the Product Backlog, and provides a long-term objective to plan against. It is not defined by requiring every stakeholder's approval or by forming a contract with the business. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Product Goal)

text: Which metrics support evidence-based product decisions in Scrum?
options: Lines of code written.
Hours worked.
Customer conversion rates.
Net Promoter Score (NPS).
trap: Lines of code and hours worked measure effort — conversion and NPS measure value.
explanation: Net Promoter Score and customer conversion rates support evidence-based product decisions because they reflect real customer response and value. Lines of code written and hours worked are activity/output measures that say nothing about delivered value. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Using a data points provided, which of the options below should you pursue? (Product A: High Current Value, Low Unrealized Value. Product B: Low Current Value, High Unrealized Value.)
options: Weight your investment toward Product B; since it has more potential.
Weight your investment toward Product A; you do not want to risk losing customers.
Put equal resources into both products.
trap: Comfort with today's strong performer (Product A) blinds you to where the growth actually is.
explanation: The best answer is to weight investment toward Product B, which has high Unrealized Value and therefore greater future opportunity. Splitting resources equally ignores that asymmetry, and favoring the mature Product A chases diminishing returns. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: Which questions does a Scrum Guide suggest all Development Team members answer at the Daily Scrum?
options: How many hours did I spend on the project yesterday?.
What work did I do yesterday to help the team achieve its goal?.
What impediments are in my way or in the way of the team?.
Why were you late?.
How is the Sprint proceeding?.
What work am I going to do today to help the team achieve its goal?.
trap: Hour counts and status interrogations turn the Daily Scrum into a report — the questions focus on the goal.
explanation: The classic Daily Scrum prompts map to what work I did yesterday to help the team meet the Sprint Goal, what work I will do today, and what impediments are in the way. The 2020 Scrum Guide no longer mandates these exact questions Developers may choose any structure - so 'hours spent', 'why were you late', and generic status prompts are not the intended focus. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 9 - Daily Scrum)

text: A Product Owner would be needed for every what?
options: A product.
All of the above.
Program.
Portfolio.
trap: One PO per product — not per program, portfolio, or 'all of the above'.
explanation: The best answer is a product. There is one Product Owner per product; a Product Owner is not defined per program or portfolio, and 'all of the above' overstates the accountability. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What does "evidence-based" mean in a context of Scrum?
options: Metrics inform prioritization.
Decisions are made based on data and outcomes.
Intuition is the only decision tool.
Plans are fixed in advance.
trap: Evidence-based means data-informed decisions — fixed plans and pure intuition are its opposites.
explanation: Being evidence-based means decisions are made on data and outcomes and that metrics inform prioritization. Fixing plans in advance or relying on intuition alone contradicts empirical process control. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism)

text: Which two activities will the Product Owner engage in during a Sprint?
options: Work with the stakeholders.
Answer questions from the Developers about Product Backlog items in the current Sprint.
Prioritize the Developers' tasks on the Sprint Backlog.
Run the Daily Scrum.
trap: Running the Daily Scrum and prioritizing Developer tasks are never PO activities.
explanation: During a Sprint the Product Owner answers the Developers' questions about Product Backlog items and works with stakeholders. Running the Daily Scrum and prioritizing the Developers' Sprint Backlog tasks belong to the self-managing Developers, not the Product Owner. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 Product Owner)

text: What would be the role of the Product Goal?
options: It replaces the Sprint Goal.
It contains the acceptance criteria.
It guides the team's work over multiple Sprints.
It defines the scope of a release.
trap: The Product Goal spans Sprints — it neither replaces Sprint Goals nor scopes a single release.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Goal guides the team's work over multiple Sprints. It is the long-term objective and the commitment for the Product Backlog - distinct from the short-term Sprint Goal, a release scope, or acceptance criteria. text: What best describes a Sprint forecast?
options: A useful tool for management to understand team performance and capacity.
Useful for the stakeholders to know what will be included in future releases.
The amount of work the Developers believe they can complete in that Sprint.
A commitment the Developers makes to deliver a particular set of Product Backlog items.
trap: A forecast is the Developers' belief, not a commitment to management or stakeholders.
explanation: The best answer is the amount of work the Developers believe they can complete in the Sprint. A forecast is an estimate based on current knowledge and capacity, not a commitment to a fixed set of items, a management performance tool, or a release promise. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning)

text: What practices are aligned with empiricism?
options: Inspecting working product frequently.
Following a fixed, approved roadmap.
Planning all features upfront.
Adapting based on usage metrics.
trap: Fixed roadmaps and fully upfront planning contradict empirical process control.
explanation: Inspecting working product frequently and adapting based on usage metrics align with empiricism. Planning all features upfront or following a fixed, approved roadmap prevent the team from learning and adapting to new information. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism)

text: What would be a benefit of frequent product releases?
options: They help teams to learn how to correct and eliminate errors.
Smaller, more frequent releases are less risky.
They enable teams to inspect and adapt more frequently.
They help teams better understand and meet customer needs.
All of the above.
None of the above.
trap: Each listed benefit is real — dismissing frequent releases with 'none of the above' is the trap.
explanation: The best answer is all of the above. Frequent releases let the team inspect and adapt more often, understand and meet customer needs, and learn to correct errors - all reinforcing empiricism and reducing risk. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 Empiricism)

text: Who builds a Product Backlog item's estimate?
options: Scrum Master.
The Development Team after clarifying requirements with the Product Owner.
The Development Team, alone.
The Product Owner with input from the Development Team.
The most senior people in the organization, including architects and subject matter experts.
trap: Estimates belong to the Developers alone — PO input informs, seniority doesn't decide.
explanation: The best answer is the Developers, alone, who will do the work and are responsible for sizing. The Product Owner may help them understand and select trade-offs, but does not make the estimate, and neither do the Scrum Master nor senior people in the organization. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 10-11 - Product Backlog)

text: An enterprise product has high daily usage but Net Promoter Score has dropped for three consecutive quarters. The sales team argues usage proves the product is successful. How should the Product Owner respond?
options: Stop releasing new features until satisfaction improves
Agree — high usage is the strongest indicator of product value
Remove the NPS metric because it conflicts with usage data
Investigate what is causing dissatisfaction despite high usage, as users may lack alternatives or be locked in
trap: High usage can mask captive, dissatisfied users — declining NPS deserves investigation, not dismissal.
explanation: The best answer is to investigate what is causing the dissatisfaction. High usage with a falling Net Promoter Score signals a value problem worth understanding empirically - not a reason to treat usage as decisive, freeze all releases, or discard the conflicting metric. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 3 - Empiricism / EBM Guide - Key Value Areas)

text: What distinguishes the Product Goal from a Sprint Goal?
options: Product Goal is short-term; Sprint Goal is long-term.
They are both synonyms in Scrum.
Sprint Goal defines the why of the Sprint; Product Goal defines long-term direction.
Sprint Goal replaces the Product Goal during development.
trap: Product Goal = long-term 'where', Sprint Goal = this Sprint's 'why' — they are neither synonyms nor substitutes.
explanation: The best answer is that the Sprint Goal defines the 'why' of the Sprint, while the Product Goal is the long-term objective for the product. They are not synonyms, the Sprint Goal is not the long-term one, and it does not replace the Product Goal during development. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 11 - Sprint Goal)

text: What usually occurs if Product Backlog items are not sufficiently clear during Sprint Planning?
options: Nothing in particular.
The Developers will have difficulty creating a forecast of work for the Sprint.
The Scrum Master should not allow this to happen. Look for a new Scrum Master and re-start the Sprint.
The meeting is cancelled so refinement can be done first.
Nothing, so long as the Product Owner gives the Developers a clear Sprint Goal.
trap: Unclear items make forecasting hard — but the meeting isn't cancelled and the SM doesn't 'forbid' it.
explanation: The best answer is that the Developers will struggle to create a realistic forecast for the Sprint. Vague items put the Sprint Goal and plan at risk; ongoing refinement prevents this. It is not harmless, nor is it the Scrum Master's job to 'not allow' it or to cancel the meeting outright. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 8-9 - Sprint Planning)

text: From the following options, which best describes the role of the Product Owner in defining Product Strategy?
options: The Product Owner manages team assignments to fit strategy.
The Product Owner is solely responsible for setting the organizational strategy.
The Product Owner has no influence over Product Strategy.
The Product Owner aligns the Product Goal with business objectives and customer needs.
trap: The PO aligns the Product Goal with business objectives — neither dictating alone nor absent from it.
explanation: The best answer is that the Product Owner aligns the Product Goal with stakeholder and customer value and orders the Product Backlog accordingly. The Product Owner is not a mere task manager, and it is inaccurate to say they have no influence over the Product Backlog - they are accountable for it. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5-6 - Product Owner)

text: What can the Product Owner do to support organizational agility?
options: Focus only on output delivery.
Avoid transparency to reduce pressure.
Promote cross-functional collaboration.
Encourage shared accountability.
trap: Focusing on output and reducing transparency shrink agility — collaboration and shared accountability grow it.
explanation: The Product Owner supports organizational agility by promoting cross-functional collaboration and encouraging shared accountability. Focusing only on output delivery or avoiding transparency to reduce pressure works against agility. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 5 - Scrum Team)

text: How much work must the Developers complete for each Product Backlog item they select for a Sprint?
options: As much as they can fit into the Sprint, with the remainder moved to the next Sprint.
Enough so that each Product Backlog item can be released.
All development work and at least some testing.
Analysis, design, programming, and testing.
trap: Each selected item must be releasable per the DoD — 'as much as fits' plus carry-over is mini-waterfall.
explanation: The best answer is: enough so that each Product Backlog item can be released. Work is only part of an Increment when it meets the Definition of Done, so each selected item must reach that releasable standard - not just 'as much as fits', or a partial slice of development and testing. (Scrum Guide 2020, p. 12 - Definition of Done)
